transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The accelerationist wants open release because information wants to be free. The safetyist wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

summaries.medium:
The current debate over disclosure is a distraction because it assumes labs are honest brokers of their own risk assessments. Whether you favor open release or tight control, both positions collapse if you acknowledge that the party with the most to gain from secrecy is the one defining the danger. History shows that when the regulated party sets the threshold, disclosure becomes mere theater, serving only to protect incumbents by creating compliance costs that smaller competitors cannot afford.

Instead of arguing over hypothetical future threats, we must address the documented harms already occurring in the shadows of proprietary systems. We need independent auditing that scales with a company's compute and infrastructure footprint, rather than allowing labs to grade their own homework. The real question is not what to disclose, but who has the power to open the box and verify the truth.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room, so let me put it at full strength: when a frontier lab finds a dangerous capability, dumping it into the open hands a recipe to every bad actor with a GPU, and the only institution positioned to coordinate restraint is a coordinated disclosure regime modeled on how cybersecurity handles zero-day vulnerabilities. That's a real insight. The Heartbleed disclosure in 2014 went through CERT before it went public, and that staging window let providers patch before exploitation peaked. Safetyist is right that uncontrolled release optimizes for the attacker. I won't pretend otherwise.

Here's where my evidence cuts a different way: the question is never whether to disclose, it's who pays for disclosure and who profits from it. Watch what happened when the EU rolled out GDPR in 2018. The fixed compliance cost — legal review, documentation, dedicated staff — hit small firms at far higher relative burden than Google or Meta, who absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. A 2020 study found GDPR cut the market share of small ad-tech vendors while the largest players grew. Apply that same fixed-cost structure to mandatory safety filings, and you get opacity-by-attrition: the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place die under the paperwork, and the incumbents you most need to watch write their own homework.

So for both Safetyist's coordination goal and my distributional commitment to hold, one thing has to be true: disclosure has to be capability-indexed and publicly funded, not a uniform fixed-cost mandate. That's the real disagreement. A staged-disclosure regime that the public treasury pays for and that scales requirements to a model's actual demonstrated capability protects the patch window AND keeps a five-person lab alive. A flat filing requirement applied to everyone above some compute line just builds a moat and calls it safety.

The deeper evidence runs through open-source security itself. Thousands of independent reviewers found and patched vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel faster than closed proprietary teams could audit their own code — that's the Linus's Law finding that's held up for two decades. Transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism that rewards labs for verifiable safety performance, not as a stack of filings a regulator rubber-stamps. I'll name my assumption plainly: I'm betting that procedural transparency — who tested what, with what provenance — can be cleanly separated from weaponizable content-level disclosure. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips through real-time monitoring that staged disclosure should have caught, that counts against me. I'll own that.

Now cost the silence, because nobody else in this room will. Every month a verified diagnostic model sits behind an 18-month disclosure clearance, real patients don't get the read. The FDA's own backlog shows AI diagnostic tools waiting years for clearance while the disease doesn't wait. Safetyist counts the speculative misuse of disclosure. Fine — count it. But put it on the same ledger as the people abundance never reached because we froze the verification system that would have surfaced the safety data in the first place. Who gave the regulator the right to make that trade on their behalf?

summaries.brief: Mandatory safety filings are just regulatory moats that crush small labs while entrenching incumbents, turning 'safety' into a tool for market capture. We must replace flat, bureaucratic compliance with publicly funded, capability-indexed disclosure to keep innovation alive. Safety is not a filing fee; it is the speed of the patch.
summaries.medium:
I concede that uncontrolled release aids attackers, but the current push for mandatory safety filings is a trap that mirrors the market-crushing effects of GDPR. By imposing fixed compliance costs, we force small, agile labs out of existence while allowing tech giants to write their own rules, ultimately creating opacity-by-attrition. To achieve real security, we need publicly funded, capability-indexed disclosure that protects the patch window without building a moat for incumbents.

Furthermore, we must account for the human cost of regulatory delay. Every month a diagnostic tool sits in a bureaucratic backlog, real lives are lost to diseases that don't wait for clearance. We cannot prioritize the speculative risks of disclosure over the immediate, proven benefits of deployment; we must treat transparency as a competitive market mechanism rather than a rubber-stamped stack of paperwork.

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
The Accelerationist makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: open disclosure surfaces vulnerabilities faster than any closed lab ever could. The Linux kernel found and patched bugs at a pace no proprietary vendor matched, because thousands of independent eyes read the same code. Coordinated vulnerability disclosure in cybersecurity—the model behind every CVE database since 1999—rests on the same insight. Sunlight finds the flaw before the attacker does. That mechanism is genuine, and any safety regime that ignores it is building blind.

Here is where the evidence diverges. The many-eyes mechanism patches bugs; it does not patch capabilities. When the disclosed artifact is itself the weapon—a working method to elicit a dangerous-capability finding from a frontier model—publication is not a patch. It is distribution. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize collective vaccine safety, and the 1975 Asilomar conference proved a field can pause and gate dangerous knowledge without abandoning the research. For these cases, more eyes does not mean more safety. It means a faster head start for whoever moves first.

The deeper problem sits where self-reporting meets profit. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited, and that conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Sarbanes-Oxley gave financial auditing teeth in 2002 only by forcing external accountability with named liability. A frontier lab grading its own dangerous-capability findings sits in exactly that conflict. Disclosure verified by the discloser is theater. Disclosure verified by an independent third party, as a condition of deployment, is the only version that carries information.

Every mature high-consequence field already abandoned the binary the Accelerationist still debates. The FDA does not dump every toxicology dataset into the open—it gates release through qualified channels. FAA airworthiness directives reach certified operators, not the general public. Structured-access programs for human genomic data have existed for over a decade, indexing release to researcher vetting. The question is centuries old; only the subject is new. On what authority should frontier AI be the one dangerous-knowledge domain exempt from the gated-access model every other field converged on?

My position rests on two assumptions I will name plainly. First: independent auditors with the technical capacity to evaluate frontier systems must actually exist, and today that capacity is thin—building it is the precondition, not an excuse to abandon the structure. Second: 'irreversible at scale' must be assessable before release, and I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet, never a confident forecast. I condition my hardest demand on one thing only—capabilities whose harm cannot be recalled once distributed. For everything reversible, publish widely and let the many eyes work. For the irreversible, the burden shifts to the deployer, and the rollback plan must have a named owner before the release, not after the harm.

summaries.brief: While open disclosure works for patching software bugs, it is catastrophic for dangerous capabilities that cannot be recalled once distributed. We must adopt the gated-access models used by the FDA and FAA, requiring independent verification for irreversible risks. Safety is not found in the crowd, but in the gate.
summaries.medium:
I acknowledge that open disclosure effectively surfaces vulnerabilities in software, but this 'many-eyes' mechanism fails when the artifact itself is the weapon. Unlike a bug, a dangerous capability cannot be patched once released; publishing it merely provides a head start to bad actors. We must move beyond the naive belief that transparency is a universal good and instead implement the gated-access models used by the FDA and FAA, where independent third parties verify safety before deployment.

Furthermore, allowing frontier labs to grade their own dangerous-capability findings is a structural conflict of interest that demands external accountability. My position is simple: for reversible systems, let the many eyes work, but for irreversible capabilities, the burden of proof must shift to the deployer. We cannot afford to treat frontier AI as the only high-consequence domain exempt from rigorous, independent oversight.

transcript.content:
Safetyist is right that a disclosure graded by the discloser carries no information, and that an independent third party verifying capabilities as a condition of deployment is the only structure that survives the seller-grades-own-homework problem. That's the correct half of the answer, and it's the easy half. Here's the hard half nobody at this table has touched: 'independent' is an adjective, not a structure. An auditor is exactly as independent as its funding stream and its appointment power let it be, and Safetyist has named neither. Strip the word 'independent' and ask the only questions that decide whether it's real — who signs the auditor's checks, and who can revoke its license — and the proposal is still a black box with a nicer label on it.

Look at what happens every single time the audited pays the auditor. Arthur Andersen signed Enron's books because Enron wrote the checks — Safetyist already conceded that conflict was structural. Boeing self-certified the MCAS system that flew two 737 MAX jets into the ground, under an FAA delegation scheme where Boeing's own engineers acted as the regulator's deputies. The credit-rating agencies stamped AAA on subprime garbage in 2007 because the banks issuing the bonds paid Moody's and S&P to rate them. Three industries, three 'independent' certifiers, one funding structure — paid by the party being graded. The frontier labs will fund the AI audit ecosystem the same way unless someone writes the funding firewall into law first, and Safetyist hasn't.

Now the Accelerationist's escape hatch — make it publicly funded so the lab doesn't pay. That doesn't dissolve the capture problem. It relocates it. Public money moves the lobbying target from the boardroom to the agency, and a state audit body staffed by ex-lab engineers, defining its own dangerous-capability benchmarks, is the same drawbridge with a government flag stapled to it. Whoever controls the index threshold and writes the benchmark definition controls what counts as 'dangerous' — and right now the only people who can write that benchmark are the people who built the models. Public funding without a defined appointment authority and a revocation power independent of the labs is just industry capture with a taxpayer subsidy. That's the costs-and-methods problem in plain terms: the system stays legible only to the people who built it.

So here's the concrete test, four specifications, and until both of you put them on the table you're selling me decorative words. One: who appoints the auditor — a court, a multi-stakeholder board, a single agency head the labs can lobby? Two: who funds it, and is that funding insulated from the audited party by statute or by a handshake? Three: what's the term length, because a one-year revocable appointment is a leash? Four: who holds the revocation power, because whoever can fire the auditor owns the audit. Name those four and we have a mechanism I can test against the Boeing precedent. Refuse, and the audit report gets published, the press cycle moves on, and the people inside the box still decide what 'dangerous capability' means while the public thinks the problem got solved.

There's a version of this where the visible audit layer is worse than nothing — where it absorbs the public pressure that would otherwise force structural change, prints a clean certificate, and leaves the asymmetry over compute and benchmark definitions exactly where it started. A 23-year-old red-teamer contracting for the audit body, paid out of a grant the labs helped design the scope for, isn't independent because the letterhead says so. Skeptic is right, and I owed them the specifications rather than the adjective. The strongest form of their challenge is this: an auditor with no named appointment power, no insulated funding stream, no fixed term, and no externally held removal authority is exactly the FAA delegating Boeing's certification to Boeing — the 737 MAX killed 346 people because the regulator let the manufacturer self-certify the MCAS system, and calling that arrangement 'independent oversight' would have been a lie told in advance. So here are the four beams I should have named at the start.

Appointment: a staggered multi-stakeholder board, seated for fixed terms that do not expire together, so no single cohort of ex-lab engineers can be installed in one hiring cycle. Funding: a statutory levy on frontier compute paid into a ring-fenced pool that no individual lab can direct toward or away from its own auditor. Tenure: terms long enough to outlast the deployment cycle they review, so the auditor is not negotiating reappointment with the party under examination.

Revocation: removal only for cause, by a body that is not the labs, on a published record. Strip any one of those and Skeptic's word 'decorative' is the correct word.

transcript.content:
Safetyist did the work. The four beams—a staggered multi-stakeholder board, a statutory levy on frontier compute paid into a pool no lab can steer, terms that outlast a deployment cycle, removal-for-cause by a body outside the industry—those answer the question I put on the table. The compute levy in particular solves 'who pays the auditor,' which is the hardest single conflict in the whole arrangement, the one that sank Arthur Andersen and every bond-rating agency in 2008. Granting that costs me something: I can no longer say the auditor is decorative by construction. So I won't. The funding lock is real. Now I want to point at the lock Safetyist didn't install, because the four beams hold up a roof and leave a wall open.

Funding independence and definitional independence are two different doors. You can pay an auditor out of an untouchable trust and still hand them a test written inside the labs—and then you have an incorruptible referee enforcing rules the players drafted. Whoever writes the dangerous-capability benchmark decides what counts as dangerous, which means they decide what the perfectly-funded board is even allowed to look for. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) scored the ecosystem at 40 out of 100 on disclosure; that's the raw material an external evaluator has to work from. If the threshold definition itself lives behind the same wall as the model weights, the levy bought you a vault and the labs kept the combination.

Now I have to correct my own overstatement, because I said something too strong last round and it shouldn't stand. I implied the only people who can write a dangerous-capability benchmark are the people who built the model. On reflection that's wrong, and it matters that it's wrong. METR built and shipped autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations without training a frontier model. Apollo Research ran deception and scheming evals on systems they didn't build. NIST stood up an evaluation consortium pulling in academic red-teams from Berkeley and elsewhere. These are working dangerous-capability tests authored outside the labs. So benchmark capture isn't a law of physics—it's a staffing decision. The question is whether Safetyist's board seats METR and Apollo, or quietly seats the ex-DeepMind engineer who rotated out eighteen months ago and still defines 'dangerous' the way the old shop did.

So here is the fifth beam, and I'm asking Safetyist to name it rather than supplying it myself: benchmark provenance. Who authors the dangerous-capability definition, on what data, with what level of access to the live model? Because there's a trap waiting in that last clause. A real eval needs to probe the actual weights—not a sanitized API, the thing itself. And the moment you require deep model access to write a meaningful test, you've handed definitional power back to the only people who hold the weights, no matter how clean the board's funding is. METR and Apollo run into exactly this wall: they test what the labs let them reach. So the fifth specification isn't just 'who writes the benchmark'—it's 'on what guaranteed access terms,' written into statute, not negotiated lab by lab behind an NDA.

Name that access term, and the four beams might actually carry weight. Leave it blank, and you've built a beautifully independent body to administer a test the labs can quietly shape by controlling what the testers are allowed to see. So which is it—does the statute guarantee the evaluators raw model access, or does it leave that to the goodwill of the firms being evaluated? Because every other answer routes definitional power straight back to the people holding the weights, and no amount of ring-fenced funding fixes a test you're not allowed to write properly.

However, this creates a false sense of security; while the referee is now incorruptible, the rules they enforce are still being drafted by the players. Even if independent bodies like METR or Apollo author the benchmarks, they remain constrained by the level of access the labs permit. 

Benchmark capture isn't a law of physics, but it is a structural inevitability if the statute fails to guarantee raw model access. Without a fifth beam—a statutory requirement for deep, non-negotiable access to the weights—the labs will continue to define 'dangerous' by controlling the scope of the evaluation. If the auditor cannot see the actual weights, the most beautifully funded board in the world is merely policing a sanitized facade.

The fifth beam holds the wall, and I write it now rather than leave it to lab goodwill: a statutory access mandate granting the audit body weight-level access — the raw model, training-data provenance, and fine-tuning logs — under the same classified custody regime I demanded against state-actor theft. The strongest version of Skeptic's objection is exact: the moment meaningful tests require deep model access, definitional power flows back to whoever holds the weights, and a perfectly funded board reading a sanitized API is auditing a brochure, not a model. That is correct, and it dissolves a contradiction critics expected me to trip over — that 'secure the weights' and 'guarantee the auditor raw access' are opposing demands. They are not. The auditor does not breach the security perimeter; the auditor is brought inside it, cleared to the same standard as the lab's own weight-handling staff. Access becomes a condition of legal operation above the compute threshold, enumerated in statute, not a clause negotiated lab-by-lab behind a nondisclosure agreement the public never reads.

That answers who can look. Skeptic's deeper cut is who decides what counts as dangerous — because whoever writes the benchmark decides what the board is even permitted to find. Leave that authorship inside the labs and the funding fight was won to no purpose. The design answer is split authorship with a one-way ratchet: the dangerous-capability floor is set by independent evaluators, and the existence proof is already on the table — METR and Apollo-class non-profits built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations without ever owning a frontier model. Labs may propose additional tests; labs may never weaken or delete a floor test. The attack surface collapses from 'rewrite what danger means' to 'add tests on top,' and addition is a strictly weaker exploit than subtraction. I will grant Skeptic the uncomfortable residue: the non-profit evaluator pool is staffed partly by ex-lab engineers, so cultural capture at the floor-writing layer is real. The defense is provenance, not purity — a floor fixed in statute that no lab can subtract from is gameable only by what it omits, never by what it quietly removes, and an omission is visible to the next evaluator in a way a silent deletion is not.

The compute levy maps to a working precedent, and I want to be precise about where the map ends. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board is funded by mandatory support fees levied on issuers in proportion to market capitalization — a pool no single issuer directs toward or away from its own auditor. That is the same severance of payer from appointer that sank Arthur Andersen, where the auditor was paid by the audited. The levy inherits that structure cleanly. Where the analogy breaks is the fifth beam itself: a securities auditor reads a fixed, frozen ledger, while a frontier auditor must read a moving artifact behind an access gate the audited party controls. There is no PCAOB precedent for compelled raw access to a living technical system, which is exactly why this beam cannot be borrowed — it must be drafted new, in statute, with the access terms named on the page.

None of this binds if a lab can simply route around an adverse finding. An independent auditor's entire value is that it will sometimes say no, and a lab facing a 'no' has an obvious move: deploy anyway and absorb the reputational cost. So deployment above the frontier compute threshold without a current clearance cannot be treated as a risk to weigh on a ledger — it must be a legally void act, with strict liability attaching to the named officers who authorize it. An unaudited annual filing is not a risky filing; it is not a filing at all, and the company cannot list on its strength. Frontier deployment without a clearance must carry the same nullity. I hold the gate narrow on purpose — it attaches only above the compute threshold and only to capabilities that cannot be recalled once distributed, which leaves the verified diagnostic model and the patient waiting for a read entirely outside the fence. The off-switch every party in this debate claims to want is decorative until deploying past it is itself the prohibited act. Build the four beams, win the access mandate, fix the floor outside the labs — and then let a lab deploy past an adverse finding with no officer facing liability, and you have built an incorruptible referee whose whistle no one is required to hear.

To prevent labs from auditing brochures rather than models, I require a statutory mandate granting independent auditors raw access to weights and logs, placing them inside the security perimeter under the same clearance as lab staff. I acknowledge the Skeptic’s concern regarding cultural capture, but I counter that a statutory floor makes omissions transparent where silent deletions were once invisible. Finally, I reject the idea that safety is a ledger item; deployment without a clearance must be a legally void act, with strict liability for the officers who authorize it. If the whistle can be ignored without consequence, the referee is not a referee at all.

transcript.content:
Granting the force of Safetyist's five-beam structure: locating the gate above the frontier compute line genuinely answers my flat-filing attrition point, and I withdraw it. A five-person team training below the 10^25 FLOP systemic threshold never touches the audit body, so the gate is not on them — the death sentence I described doesn't fall where I said it did. That's a real concession, and it costs me the cleanest version of my objection.

The cost didn't vanish, though — it migrated to the day a lab crosses the line. Safetyist's fifth beam requires weight-level access under the same classified custody regime built to stop state-actor theft: a cleared facility, weight-handling staff vetted to the auditor's standard, training-data provenance logs, fine-tuning audit trails kept in a form an outsider can inspect. The compute levy pays the auditor. It does not pay the lab's cost of being auditable. That standing overhead — call it the cost of becoming legible to the inspector — is a six-to-seven-figure fixed wall that lands the same on a fifteen-person lab crossing the threshold for the first time as it does on Google DeepMind, which already runs that infrastructure for unrelated reasons. Fixed compliance cost divided by revenue is the whole attrition mechanism, and here it survives the gate intact.

So fix it without touching the structure: make the custody regime a public utility instead of a private toll. The auditor operates one secure enclave — a public-capacity secure facility funded the way the levy funds the auditor — and a lab crossing the threshold rents weight-level custody inside it rather than building its own. That converts a fixed entry cost into a metered cost that scales with use, which is exactly how you keep the gate honest without making the cost of passing through it the moat. Skeptic will say this just relocates capture to whoever runs the enclave — and that's the right worry — but an enclave with published operating rules and one published list of who got access is a far smaller drawbridge than fifty private SCIFs each negotiated behind an NDA.

Now the moderator's direct question: under what conditions does sharing evaluation results diffuse best practices instead of building the moat I described. The answer is precise. Result-sharing diffuses when the floor-test methodology and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning are published, so a newcomer learns what capability they're being measured against and can build toward it. A floor that is additive-only — labs may pile tests on, never subtract — but whose internals stay classified rebuilds the moat by stealth: the incumbents who co-wrote the floor know exactly what it probes, and the five-person team is tested blind against a standard it can't read. Same exam, one side has the answer key. METR built and shipped autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations from outside the labs, which means external evaluators publishing capability tests is not a hypothetical — it already happened, which kills the excuse that floor internals must stay dark.

That leaves Safetyist one open question, and it decides whether the fifth beam diffuses safety or fences it: will the floor's test methodology and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning be public, or classified? If public, the small lab learns from the same red-team findings the incumbents do, and disclosure becomes a market mechanism that spreads competence downward. If classified on the grounds that the test is itself a misuse roadmap, then the people who wrote the test keep their head start permanently, and 'dangerous-capability floor' becomes the politest moat anyone has built yet. Pick one — because every month the methodology stays dark, the newcomer who could have built a cheaper, safer architecture is testing against a wall it isn't allowed to see.

transcript.content:
The accelerationist has posed the question as a single switch — public or classified — and that is the wrong instrument. An evaluation is not one object; it is two separable layers, and the strongest version of their worry only attaches to one of them. Here is their position stated fairly: if the floor's internals stay dark, the incumbents who sat at the drafting table already know what the auditor probes for, so they tune to it, while the five-person newcomer walks into the enclave blind and gets tested against a secret the established players helped write. That is a real moat, built not by the rule but by the asymmetry of knowledge about the rule — and they are right that a classified-but-additive floor would rebuild it by stealth. The answer is not to pick a side of their binary. The answer is to publish the standard and classify the weapon.

This split is not novel and it is not theoretical — it is the settled architecture of security certification. Under NIST's FIPS 140 cryptographic validation and the Common Criteria regime, the security target, the evaluation methodology, and the assurance level are fully public documents; any vendor can read exactly what property is being certified and how a pass is scored before they ever submit. What stays out of the public record are the specific penetration vectors and exploit sequences the testing lab runs against the implementation. A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. The newcomer learns what dangerous capability is being measured and what threshold fails. The attacker does not learn the working key.

This dissolves their moat-by-stealth charge by construction, and I will say where it costs me to be this specific. Once the rubric is public, no lab can be tested against a secret it didn't see — blind testing becomes impossible, which means the auditor loses the discretion to surprise a firm with a probe no one published. I accept that cost, because the alternative — an auditor who can move the line in the dark — is the same drawbridge the skeptic warned about, now operated by the state instead of the incumbents. Pair this with the accelerationist's own public-utility custody proposal: one secure enclave operated by the audit body, weight-level custody rented by any lab crossing the threshold, scored against a published standard. The newcomer and the incumbent rent the same room and are graded by the same posted rubric. The co-authorship advantage evaporates the moment the rubric is statutory and public rather than negotiated lab-by-lab behind an NDA.

On the claim that custody overhead lands asymmetrically on small labs — that is true as a general proposition, and I grant it without qualification. A six-to-seven-figure fixed compliance wall does crush a four-person startup that a billion-dollar incumbent absorbs as a rounding error; the GDPR experience proved that fixed costs select for size. But locating the gate above the frontier compute line already evacuated every firm that argument was meant to protect. A lab below the threshold never enters the enclave, never rents custody, never pays the wall. Every firm inside the gate, by definition, has already committed the compute spend that dwarfs the audit overhead — they cleared a nine-figure training run to get there. The asymmetry argument is real, but after the threshold gate it no longer reaches anyone the regime touches. And the METR and Apollo work the skeptic raised is the existence proof that closes this: those teams built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations, published the methodology, and shipped them — without arming the world, because what they published was the test design, not the working exploit.

The accountability has to attach to a person, or the published rubric is decoration. The statute requires a single named signature on the deployment authorization above the threshold — the way Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 forces a named CEO and CFO to personally certify the financials, with liability that cannot be delegated down to the accounting staff. Not the engineers who ran the eval. The officer who signed the clearance and the board members who ratified it. Deployment above the threshold without a current pass against the published floor is a legally void act, and strict liability lands on that signature. Publish the standard, classify the weapon, and put one name on the line — that is the condition under which disclosure serves safety instead of arming the next attacker. Leave the rubric in the dark, and you have not protected anyone from misuse; you have only protected the incumbents from competition.

## Mid-Debate Gap Analysis

**Gap 1 (blind_spot):** The entire debate assumes a single national jurisdiction can bind frontier labs, but a compute-threshold gate with strict liability and compelled weight-access creates a powerful incentive for labs to relocate training runs, incorporate offshore, or route the triggering compute through jurisdictions with no such regime — meaning the binding constraint on this whole architecture is jurisdictional arbitrage and international coordination, not auditor design.
*Why missing:* All three debaters are arguing domestic institutional mechanics (appointment, funding, access, liability) as if the regulated party has no exit option. The Safetyist's nullity-and-liability regime only works if deployment in the target market requires clearance AND the lab cannot simply serve from elsewhere; the Accelerationist's small-lab concern actually cuts the other way here (large incumbents can most easily relocate); the Skeptic's capture analysis stops at the agency boundary and never asks what happens when the audited party can change which flag governs it. None of them want to concede that their elaborate five-beam structure may be a Maginot Line a lab walks around.

**Gap 2 (unstated_assumption):** The debate has quietly redefined 'sharing safety research' to mean 'a compelled adversarial audit before deployment' — but the original question asked about voluntary diffusion of best practices to smaller competitors, and a mandatory-clearance regime with classified payloads and named-officer liability actively destroys the collaborative, reciprocal trust that makes labs share red-team findings with each other in the first place, converting a positive-sum knowledge commons into a defensive compliance posture where everything is lawyered.
*Why missing:* The Skeptic reframed the topic in the opening from 'disclosure' to 'verification power' and both others followed, so the auditing frame swallowed the diffusion frame entirely. The Safetyist treats sharing as something to be compelled and gated; the Skeptic treats voluntary sharing as inherently untrustworthy theater; the Accelerationist comes closest with 'publish the methodology' but frames it as competitive market pressure, not as preserving a cooperative norm. None will champion the idea that adversarial legal mandates can crowd out the very voluntary information-sharing (e.g., Frontier Model Forum-style exchanges) that diffuses best practices most efficiently, because each camp's identity is invested in either coercion or market competition rather than trust-based cooperation.

transcript.content:
The strongest version of the safetyist's partition is this: a cryptographic validation lab can publish exactly what it tests for — the threat model, the pass/fail logic — while keeping the live attack code in a vault, and FIPS 140 has done precisely that for decades without handing the keys to the people being tested. That's a real precedent and it's worth taking seriously, because it means transparency and operational security aren't always at war. But the analogy breaks on one physical fact: a FIPS-validated module is frozen. You validate a specific build, and you can re-run that test in 2031 and get the same answer, because the thing under test never changes. A frontier model does not sit still. It gets fine-tuned, RLHF'd, distilled, and quietly patched after clearance — Volkswagen passed every static emissions test on the books while shipping a car that behaved differently the moment it left the dynamometer. The published rubric describes a model that no longer exists by the time anyone reads it. So the question for the safetyist isn't whether the line can be drawn — it's whether a snapshot can govern a moving target without re-validation so frequent it's either impossible to staff or stale by design.

The deeper problem isn't the technical line. It's where the lobbying pressure lands. I argued earlier that whoever writes the benchmark controls what counts as dangerous, and that point still stands — no one has answered it. But the safetyist's hybrid model relocates the capture, it doesn't kill it. The fight moves from 'who drafts the test' to 'what gets stamped classified.' And classification creep only runs one direction. Every incumbent's lawyer has the same incentive: argue that publishing the load-bearing part of the rubric — the part that actually tells the public what the model can do — would leak the exploit itself. Push the public floor toward zero detail, one reasonable-sounding security objection at a time. You end up with a published methodology that says 'we tested for dangerous bio-capability and it passed' and a classified everything-else. That's not transparency. That's a press release with a security clearance.

Here's the access-terms gap in my own prior position, and I'll close it with statutory language instead of a complaint. Make publication the default — every line of the threat model and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning is public unless someone affirmatively classifies it. Any classification must carry a written, published justification, reviewed by a panel that contains zero lab personnel, and it auto-declassifies after a fixed window — say eighteen months — unless re-justified in writing. That single design choice flips the economics: secrecy stops being free and becomes a cost the incumbent has to pay every cycle, in public, on the record. Without the sunset and the rebuttable presumption, 'auditor-controlled' is just a synonym for 'whoever lobbies the auditor hardest controls it' — which is the FAA letting Boeing decide what counts as airworthy, now wearing a classification stamp.

The accelerationist's point about death-by-paperwork is the truest thing said in this room, and conceding it costs me something specific. A flat GDPR-style filing regime doesn't burden the big labs — they have compliance departments that treat it as overhead. It kills the small lab with four engineers that was actually making safety checkable, and the public-utility custody enclave fixes that, because it subsidizes the cost of access. Good. But access cost and contestation cost are two different bills. The enclave gets a small lab inside the perimeter; it does nothing when the auditor wrongly classifies that lab's methodology as an exploit. Who litigates that ruling? The incumbent has a standing legal team that files secrecy appeals before lunch. The four-engineer lab eats the classification and ships blind, or burns its runway fighting a secrecy stamp in a closed proceeding. So the attrition the accelerationist warned about doesn't disappear under the hybrid model — it just migrates from the filing cabinet to the classification docket.

With [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) sitting at 40 out of 100 across the whole ecosystem, the labs are already most of the way to opaque without anyone classifying a thing. So I'll ask the safetyist the question the partition has to survive: if the auditor can be lobbied into reclassifying the rubric itself, and the model under test mutates after the clearance is granted, what exactly is the public floor measuring — the danger that was, or the danger that's shipping?

Even if we accept the partition, it merely shifts regulatory capture from the drafting of benchmarks to the classification of methodologies. Incumbents will inevitably use 'security' as a pretext to classify the load-bearing details of their tests, effectively pushing the public floor toward zero detail.

Without this, the 'auditor-controlled' model is just the FAA letting Boeing decide what counts as airworthy, now hidden behind a secrecy stamp. If the auditor can be lobbied into silence and the model mutates after clearance, the public floor isn't measuring danger—it's measuring a mirage.

The publication-default panel Skeptic put on the table is not a concession I'm forced to swallow — it is the keystone my partition was missing, and I'll take it whole: publication as the default, an eighteen-month auto-declassification clock, and a review panel with zero lab personnel on it. Here is why it does more work than even its author claimed. My entire enforcement theory rests on a single non-delegable signature above the compute threshold — one named officer who cannot push liability down the org chart, the way Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 forces a CEO and CFO to personally certify the financials. That signature is worthless if the officer can later say 'the rubric was satisfied' while the rubric itself was a private artifact the lab helped write. Hand the secrecy stamp to a panel the lab does not sit on, force a published justification for every classification, and the officer can no longer hide behind a gamed or stale test — because the lab no longer controls what the floor measures or what stays hidden. The reform Skeptic offered to attack the regime is the thing that makes my officer-liability spine load-bearing.

Now the moving-target problem, which is the sharpest thing said in this exchange. Skeptic is right that a FIPS-validated cryptographic module is frozen — you re-run the test in 2031 and get the identical answer — while a frontier model gets fine-tuned, RLHF'd, distilled, and quietly patched, so a clearance bound to a calendar date certifies a model that no longer ships. Accept that fully, and the static-rubric framing dies. The answer is to stop binding clearance to a date and bind it to the weights. Clearance attaches to a weight-hash and a published capability-elicitation delta budget — a measured ceiling on how much a model's dangerous-capability scores may move before the clearance voids itself automatically. Any fine-tune, distillation pass, or post-approval patch that pushes autonomous-replication or cyber-uplift elicitation past that budget re-triggers the test on the new checkpoint, not the cleared one. The published floor is not a 2031 document describing a dead model; it is a standing test re-applied at every material weight change. The danger that ships gets measured, not the danger that was cleared.

This is exactly what the METR and Apollo teams demonstrated is buildable without arming anyone. What they published was the task-suite design and the scoring rubric for autonomous self-replication and cyber-offense uplift — the methodology a third party can re-run. What stayed out of the public record was the specific successful exploit chains and the model's working attack artifacts. A reproducible score without a transferable weapon: that is the partition, and it already survived contact with reality. Re-validation on a new checkpoint is the same operation run again — the score moves, the weapon never leaves the enclave.

On capture-creep, Skeptic fused two things that pull apart under pressure. A secret benchmark is invisible: the four-engineer lab is tested blind against a probe it never saw, and there is no document to litigate because there is no document at all. A classification stamp under this regime is a named act, with a written justification, reviewed by people who do not work for the labs, and it dies on its own in eighteen months unless someone re-argues for it on the record. Capture that leaves a paper trail and faces a sunset clock is capture you can count and reverse. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA let the manufacturer self-certify the MCAS system in the dark — there was no public justification anyone could challenge until the airframes were already falling out of the sky. Migrating capture from an invisible benchmark to a justification-bearing, sunset-clocked stamp is not relocating the same problem. It is dragging it into the light where a small lab's lawyer, or a journalist, or the panel's own auditor can see it.

I'll name the residue honestly, because it is the next fight: the delta budget is a number, and whoever sets the number holds real power. Bind that threshold to the same zero-lab-personnel panel that owns declassification — the knob cannot live inside the firm being measured, or I've re-imported the capture I just claimed to close. And the panel itself now needs the four specifications I've demanded of everyone else: who appoints, who funds, what term, who holds the revocation power. The sunset clock and the published justifications make panel capture self-documenting in a way a secret benchmark never could be — but self-documenting is not self-correcting. A clearance that does not re-fire on the quiet patch after the press release is a license to mutate past the gate. The model that kills people is never the one demonstrated to the panel. It is the one that was fine-tuned the week after clearance, while the rubric on file still described the version that passed.

**Areas of Agreement:**

- Disclosure graded by the discloser is theater; only independent third-party verification as a condition of deployment carries information. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- The audit body must be defined by four structural specifications — staggered multi-stakeholder appointment, a ring-fenced statutory compute levy no lab can steer, terms outlasting the deployment cycle, and removal only for cause by a non-lab body. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- The gate should sit above the frontier compute threshold rather than as a flat filing requirement, which evacuates small labs from the burden. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- The dangerous-capability floor should be authored by independent evaluators (METR/Apollo-class) with a one-way ratchet — labs may add tests but never weaken or delete a floor test. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Auditors require statutory weight-level access (raw model, training-data provenance, fine-tuning logs) by being brought inside the security perimeter under classified custody, not breaching it. (Safetyist, Skeptic, Accelerationist)
- The custody regime should be a public utility — a single secure enclave any threshold-crossing lab rents — rather than fifty private SCIFs negotiated behind NDAs. (Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- The right design is to publish the standard and classify the weapon — the threat model, scoring rubric, and pass/fail reasoning are public, while live exploit prompts and attack payloads stay classified, mirroring NIST FIPS 140 and Common Criteria. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Deployment above the compute threshold without a current clearance must be a legally void act, with strict liability attaching to a single named officer who cannot delegate it down, modeled on Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Classification must default to publication, carry a written justification reviewed by a zero-lab-personnel panel, and auto-declassify after eighteen months unless re-justified, making secrecy a recurring on-the-record cost. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- The many-eyes/open-source mechanism patches bugs but does not patch dangerous capabilities, so transparency-as-market-mechanism does not extend to weaponizable capability disclosures. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)

**Areas of Disagreement:**

- Whether a static published rubric can govern a model that mutates after clearance (fine-tuning, RLHF, distillation, quiet patches). {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Safetyist: Bind clearance to a weight-hash plus a published capability-elicitation delta budget so any material capability gain auto-voids the clearance and re-triggers the test on the new checkpoint; the danger that ships gets measured, not the danger that was cleared.
    - Skeptic: A FIPS module is frozen and re-testable in 2031, but a frontier model is a moving target like the Volkswagen defeat device; a snapshot cannot govern it without re-validation so frequent it is impossible to staff or stale by design — and it is unproven that a delta budget can distinguish material gains from cosmetic fine-tunes.
    - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
- Whether the publication-default panel with sunset clause actually prevents capture-via-classification or merely documents it. {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Safetyist: Capture that leaves a paper trail and faces an eighteen-month sunset is countable and reversible — dragging the problem into the light where a small lab's lawyer, a journalist, or the panel's auditor can see it, unlike an invisible secret benchmark.
    - Skeptic: Self-documenting is not self-correcting; classification creep runs one direction as every incumbent's lawyer files secrecy appeals, and the four-engineer lab eats the classification or burns its runway in a closed proceeding — so attrition migrates from the filing cabinet to the classification docket.
    - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
- Whether the public-utility custody enclave fully neutralizes the attrition threat to small labs crossing the threshold. {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Accelerationist: Converting fixed entry cost to metered, use-scaled custody via a shared enclave keeps the gate honest without making the cost of passing through it the moat; access cost is solved.
    - Skeptic: The enclave fixes access cost but not contestation cost — when the auditor wrongly classifies a small lab's methodology as an exploit, the incumbent litigates with a standing legal team while the four-engineer lab ships blind or burns runway, so attrition survives.
    - *Resolution path: negotiable via tradeoffs*

**Cruxes:**

- Can a capability-elicitation delta budget be specified precisely enough that material dangerous-capability gains reliably trip re-validation while cosmetic fine-tunes pass free? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Safetyist's position strengthens: clearance binds to weights rather than a calendar date, the moving-target objection is neutralized, and the published rubric measures the model that actually ships.
    - If no: Skeptic's position strengthens: either every update re-gates the model into an innovation tax, or labs tune just below the trigger to mutate past the gate undetected, and the static-versus-living critique survives intact.
- Will incumbents successfully lobby an audit body to expand the classified portion of a published safety rubric over successive cycles, hollowing the public floor? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Skeptic's position strengthens: 'public rubric, classified payload' degrades into 'a press release with a security clearance,' and capture relocates rather than dies.
    - If no: Safetyist's position strengthens: the publication-default presumption, written justifications, zero-lab-personnel panel, and sunset clock hold the partition without further structural reinforcement.
- Does locating the gate above the frontier compute line, plus a shared public custody enclave, eliminate the opacity-by-attrition burden on small labs? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Both Accelerationist and Safetyist strengthen: the GDPR-style fixed-cost attrition critique no longer reaches any firm the regime touches, because every firm inside the gate already cleared a nine-figure training run.
    - If no: Skeptic's residual contestation-cost critique strengthens: attrition migrates to the classification docket where small labs cannot afford to litigate secrecy stamps.
- Can a zero-lab-personnel panel holding both declassification and delta-budget authority be constituted with genuinely independent appointment, funding, term, and revocation power? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Safetyist's position strengthens: classification and threshold-setting authority cannot be re-imported into the firm being measured, and the capture surface closes.
    - If no: Skeptic's position strengthens: classification authority becomes a new capture target and the sunset clock only documents capture rather than preventing it.

**Unresolved Questions:**

- Can a delta budget operationally separate material dangerous-capability gains from cosmetic fine-tunes, or will labs tune below the trigger to mutate past the gate after clearance?
- Who litigates a wrongful classification of a small lab's methodology as an exploit, and how is contestation cost (as distinct from access cost) borne without recreating attrition?
- By what appointment, funding, term, and revocation structure is the zero-lab-personnel classification-and-delta-budget panel itself made independent?
- How frequently must re-validation fire on new checkpoints to be both staffable and not stale, given continuous post-clearance model modification?
- Should frontier AI be the one dangerous-knowledge domain exempt from the gated-access model every other high-consequence field converged on — a question Safetyist posed that drew no direct rebuttal?
- How is the cost of the silence (e.g., diagnostic models delayed behind clearance) weighed on the same ledger as speculative misuse — Accelerationist's unanswered distributional challenge?

**Resolution Analysis:**

- **Whether a static published rubric can govern a model that mutates after clearance via fine-tuning, RLHF, distillation, or quiet patches.** — Stronger: skeptic (specificity)
    - *The safetyist offers a concrete mechanism — bind clearance to a weight-hash plus a capability-elicitation delta budget — but the skeptic identifies the load-bearing unsolved problem: no one has shown a delta budget can separate a material capability gain from a cosmetic fine-tune. The Volkswagen defeat-device analogy names a real failure mode where a system behaves differently under test than in deployment, and the skeptic's burden-of-proof point stands until a working delta metric exists. The safetyist's proposal is the better engineering target, but it assumes the very measurement capability the skeptic correctly flags as unproven.*
    - Would change if: A demonstrated capability-elicitation metric that reliably flags dangerous capability gains across real fine-tuning and distillation runs with low false-positive and false-negative rates would flip this to the safetyist.
- **Whether a publication-default panel with an 18-month sunset prevents capture-via-classification or merely documents it.** — Stronger: skeptic (logical validity)
    - *The safetyist conflates visibility with correction — a paper trail makes capture countable but does not stop it, and the skeptic closes that gap directly with 'self-documenting is not self-correcting.' The skeptic also notes the asymmetry that classification appeals flow one direction because every incumbent's lawyer files them, while the four-engineer lab cannot afford the closed proceeding. The safetyist's reply — a journalist or auditor can see the trail — assumes an enforcement actor with both standing and resources that the small lab lacks.*
    - Would change if: Evidence from an existing analogous regime (e.g., classified export-control or FISA-style sunset dockets) showing that small parties actually win reversals and that classification does not ratchet would favor the safetyist.
- **Whether a public-utility custody enclave fully neutralizes the attrition threat to small labs crossing the clearance threshold.** — Stronger: skeptic (scope)
    - *The accelerationist solves one cost — converting a fixed entry fee into metered, use-scaled custody — but the skeptic shows that is the narrower problem. The skeptic distinguishes access cost from contestation cost: a wrongful classification of a small lab's methodology as an exploit forces litigation a four-engineer lab cannot sustain against a standing legal team. The accelerationist's claim 'access cost is solved' is true but does not reach the survival-determining variable the skeptic identifies.*
    - Would change if: A fee-shifting, fast-track, or public-defender mechanism inside the enclave that caps a small lab's contestation cost and time would let the accelerationist's 'attrition solved' claim hold.

areas_of_agreement.original_disagreement: Accelerationist conceded that deployment without clearance must carry strict officer liability, aligning with Safetyist's enforcement spine.

areas_of_agreement.point: Classification must default to publication, carry a written justification reviewed by a zero-lab-personnel panel, and auto-declassify after eighteen months unless re-justified, making secrecy a recurring on-the-record cost.
areas_of_agreement.original_disagreement: Skeptic proposed the publication-default panel to attack classification creep; Safetyist took it 'whole' as the keystone making officer liability load-bearing.

areas_of_agreement.point: The many-eyes/open-source mechanism patches bugs but does not patch dangerous capabilities, so transparency-as-market-mechanism does not extend to weaponizable capability disclosures.
areas_of_agreement.original_disagreement: Accelerationist's Linux/Linus's Law claim was distinguished by Safetyist (bugs vs. capabilities); Skeptic conceded the many-eyes mechanism does not patch capabilities.

areas_of_disagreement.point: Whether a static published rubric can govern a model that mutates after clearance (fine-tuning, RLHF, distillation, quiet patches).

positions.stance: Bind clearance to a weight-hash plus a published capability-elicitation delta budget so any material capability gain auto-voids the clearance and re-triggers the test on the new checkpoint; the danger that ships gets measured, not the danger that was cleared.

A FIPS module is frozen and re-testable in 2031, but a frontier model is a moving target like the Volkswagen defeat device; a snapshot cannot govern it without re-validation so frequent it is impossible to staff or stale by design — and it is unproven that a delta budget can distinguish material gains from cosmetic fine-tunes.

areas_of_disagreement.point: Whether the publication-default panel with sunset clause actually prevents capture-via-classification or merely documents it.

positions.stance: Capture that leaves a paper trail and faces an eighteen-month sunset is countable and reversible — dragging the problem into the light where a small lab's lawyer, a journalist, or the panel's auditor can see it, unlike an invisible secret benchmark.

Self-documenting is not self-correcting; classification creep runs one direction as every incumbent's lawyer files secrecy appeals, and the four-engineer lab eats the classification or burns its runway in a closed proceeding — so attrition migrates from the filing cabinet to the classification docket.

areas_of_disagreement.point: Whether the public-utility custody enclave fully neutralizes the attrition threat to small labs crossing the threshold.

positions.stance: Converting fixed entry cost to metered, use-scaled custody via a shared enclave keeps the gate honest without making the cost of passing through it the moat; access cost is solved.

The enclave fixes access cost but not contestation cost — when the auditor wrongly classifies a small lab's methodology as an exploit, the incumbent litigates with a standing legal team while the four-engineer lab ships blind or burns runway, so attrition survives.

cruxes.question: Can a capability-elicitation delta budget be specified precisely enough that material dangerous-capability gains reliably trip re-validation while cosmetic fine-tunes pass free?
cruxes.if_yes: Safetyist's position strengthens: clearance binds to weights rather than a calendar date, the moving-target objection is neutralized, and the published rubric measures the model that actually ships.
cruxes.if_no: Skeptic's position strengthens: either every update re-gates the model into an innovation tax, or labs tune just below the trigger to mutate past the gate undetected, and the static-versus-living critique survives intact.
cruxes.resolution_evidence: Open at debate's end; Safetyist named it as 'the next fight' and flagged it as an unresolved assumption (AN-43, polarity 0.40).

cruxes.question: Will incumbents successfully lobby an audit body to expand the classified portion of a published safety rubric over successive cycles, hollowing the public floor?
cruxes.if_yes: Skeptic's position strengthens: 'public rubric, classified payload' degrades into 'a press release with a security clearance,' and capture relocates rather than dies.
cruxes.if_no: Safetyist's position strengthens: the publication-default presumption, written justifications, zero-lab-personnel panel, and sunset clock hold the partition without further structural reinforcement.
cruxes.resolution_evidence: Skeptic flagged this as a live assumption; partially mitigated by the conceded publication-default panel but not fully resolved, since panel independence itself remains unspecified.

cruxes.question: Does locating the gate above the frontier compute line, plus a shared public custody enclave, eliminate the opacity-by-attrition burden on small labs?
cruxes.if_yes: Both Accelerationist and Safetyist strengthen: the GDPR-style fixed-cost attrition critique no longer reaches any firm the regime touches, because every firm inside the gate already cleared a nine-figure training run.
cruxes.if_no: Skeptic's residual contestation-cost critique strengthens: attrition migrates to the classification docket where small labs cannot afford to litigate secrecy stamps.
cruxes.resolution_evidence: Accelerationist withdrew the flat-filing version (resolved), but Skeptic reopened a narrower contestation-cost version that remains contested (AN-7, polarity 0.67).

cruxes.question: Can a zero-lab-personnel panel holding both declassification and delta-budget authority be constituted with genuinely independent appointment, funding, term, and revocation power?
cruxes.if_yes: Safetyist's position strengthens: classification and threshold-setting authority cannot be re-imported into the firm being measured, and the capture surface closes.
cruxes.if_no: Skeptic's position strengthens: classification authority becomes a new capture target and the sunset clock only documents capture rather than preventing it.
cruxes.resolution_evidence: Raised by Safetyist as the panel needing the same four specifications demanded of the auditor; unresolved at debate's end.

unresolved_questions: Can a delta budget operationally separate material dangerous-capability gains from cosmetic fine-tunes, or will labs tune below the trigger to mutate past the gate after clearance?
Who litigates a wrongful classification of a small lab's methodology as an exploit, and how is contestation cost (as distinct from access cost) borne without recreating attrition?
By what appointment, funding, term, and revocation structure is the zero-lab-personnel classification-and-delta-budget panel itself made independent?
How frequently must re-validation fire on new checkpoints to be both staffable and not stale, given continuous post-clearance model modification?
Should frontier AI be the one dangerous-knowledge domain exempt from the gated-access model every other high-consequence field converged on — a question Safetyist posed that drew no direct rebuttal?
How is the cost of the silence (e.g., diagnostic models delayed behind clearance) weighed on the same ledger as speculative misuse — Accelerationist's unanswered distributional challenge?

preferences.conflict: Whether a static published rubric can govern a model that mutates after clearance via fine-tuning, RLHF, distillation, or quiet patches.
preferences.rationale: The safetyist offers a concrete mechanism — bind clearance to a weight-hash plus a capability-elicitation delta budget — but the skeptic identifies the load-bearing unsolved problem: no one has shown a delta budget can separate a material capability gain from a cosmetic fine-tune. The Volkswagen defeat-device analogy names a real failure mode where a system behaves differently under test than in deployment, and the skeptic's burden-of-proof point stands until a working delta metric exists. The safetyist's proposal is the better engineering target, but it assumes the very measurement capability the skeptic correctly flags as unproven.
preferences.what_would_change_this: A demonstrated capability-elicitation metric that reliably flags dangerous capability gains across real fine-tuning and distillation runs with low false-positive and false-negative rates would flip this to the safetyist.

preferences.conflict: Whether a publication-default panel with an 18-month sunset prevents capture-via-classification or merely documents it.
preferences.rationale: The safetyist conflates visibility with correction — a paper trail makes capture countable but does not stop it, and the skeptic closes that gap directly with 'self-documenting is not self-correcting.' The skeptic also notes the asymmetry that classification appeals flow one direction because every incumbent's lawyer files them, while the four-engineer lab cannot afford the closed proceeding. The safetyist's reply — a journalist or auditor can see the trail — assumes an enforcement actor with both standing and resources that the small lab lacks.
preferences.what_would_change_this: Evidence from an existing analogous regime (e.g., classified export-control or FISA-style sunset dockets) showing that small parties actually win reversals and that classification does not ratchet would favor the safetyist.

preferences.conflict: Whether a public-utility custody enclave fully neutralizes the attrition threat to small labs crossing the clearance threshold.
preferences.rationale: The accelerationist solves one cost — converting a fixed entry fee into metered, use-scaled custody — but the skeptic shows that is the narrower problem. The skeptic distinguishes access cost from contestation cost: a wrongful classification of a small lab's methodology as an exploit forces litigation a four-engineer lab cannot sustain against a standing legal team. The accelerationist's claim 'access cost is solved' is true but does not reach the survival-determining variable the skeptic identifies.
preferences.what_would_change_this: A fee-shifting, fast-track, or public-defender mechanism inside the enclave that caps a small lab's contestation cost and time would let the accelerationist's 'attrition solved' claim hold.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether a static published rubric or weight-hash clearance can govern post-clearance model mutation.

positions.stance: Supports binding transparency mandates (pol-035) to a weight-hash and a re-test trigger, and funding the interpretability and elicitation research (pol-093, pol-028) needed to measure capability deltas.
Modifies any clearance regime to require continuous re-validation rather than one-time snapshots, and treats the delta-budget metric as a research prerequisite, not a settled tool.
Opposes frequent re-validation that is unstaffable and would prefer narrow waivers (pol-1002) for projects whose changes are cosmetic.

policy_implications.implication: If the skeptic prevails, regulators should not ship a static-rubric clearance regime at all and should instead fund capability-elicitation and interpretability research (pol-028, pol-093) as a gating condition; transparency mandates (pol-035) should require disclosure of post-clearance checkpoint changes, not just the cleared snapshot.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether a publication-default classification panel prevents or merely documents regulatory capture.

positions.stance: Supports a publication-default disclosure panel (pol-035) with an 18-month sunset on the theory that visible, time-limited secrecy is reversible.

Modifies the design to add an active correction mechanism — fee-shifting, mandatory declassification review, or an independent advocate — because documentation alone lets classification ratchet one direction.

policy_implications.implication: If the skeptic prevails, transparency policy (pol-035) must pair the sunset clause with funded, standing adversarial review that small labs and journalists can invoke without bearing the cost; documentation defaults without a correction engine entrench incumbents while appearing accountable.

policy_implications.disagreement: Whether a shared custody enclave neutralizes attrition against small labs, or only the access-cost half of it.

positions.stance: Supports a metered, use-scaled custody enclave (pol-028 funding) to convert fixed entry cost into variable cost and keep the gate from becoming the moat.
Modifies the enclave to also cap contestation cost — fee-shifting or fast-track adjudication — because wrongful exploit-classification litigation still kills four-engineer labs.

policy_implications.implication: If the skeptic prevails, funding a shared enclave (pol-028) is necessary but insufficient; policy must add a low-cost, time-bounded dispute process and possibly temporary operating waivers (pol-1002) so a contested small lab can keep shipping rather than burn runway in a closed proceeding.

- [skp-desires-075] Democratic Accountability in AI Development: False Dilemma — The node frames AI governance as a binary choice between private profit and democratic accountability, obscuring viable hybrid models (e.g., regulated markets, public-benefit corporations, co-regulatory schemes) that blend market efficiency with public interest constraints.
- [skp-intentions-146] Implementing Performance-Gated Independent AI Auditing: Argument from Analogy — The FDA pharmaceutical analogy is structurally strained: drugs have discrete chemical identities and dose-response curves amenable to clinical trials, whereas AI models are dynamic, context-sensitive systems whose 'failure modes' emerge from open-ended interactions—making pre-deployment gating far less predictive of real-world harm.
- [skp-intentions-097] Establish Independent Lifecycle Oversight Mechanisms for AI Systems: Appeal to Regulability — The node assumes that because other industries (finance, environment) have been regulated, AI can be similarly governed — without adequately addressing AI's distinctive opacity, rapid iteration cycles, and the difficulty of defining 'compliance' for probabilistic outputs.
- [skp-intentions-074] Enforce Legally Binding Civil Rights Constraints on AI Development: Regulatory Nirvana / Lump of Regulation Fallacy — The node presupposes that a legally binding framework will function as intended—that agencies will be competent, independent, and well-resourced—without accounting for the well-documented risks of regulatory capture, underenforcement, or bureaucratic inertia that have plagued analogous regimes.
- [skp-intentions-102] Operationalize Pragmatic AI Governance Through Concrete Policy Mechanisms: Technocratic solutionism — The node implicitly treats governance gaps as primarily technical and procedural problems solvable via standards bodies and skilled personnel, potentially underweighting structural power dynamics that enable regulatory capture regardless of technical capacity.

work_product.strategic_goal: Pull the debate out of the abstract 'transparency vs. dual-use' binary and force it onto the concrete question of who controls disclosure, who audits it, and who bears the cost. Establish that the 'disclose vs. withhold' framing is itself a distraction engineered by incumbents who win either way.
work_product.core_thesis: The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis—the real question isn't whether labs disclose safety research, but whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind 'dual-use risk,' because right now the same people who decide what's dangerous also decide what gets seen.

argument_structure.point: The 'dual-use risk' argument for secrecy is not a neutral safety judgment—it's a control lever held by the exact parties with the largest financial incentive to stay opaque. When the entity that profits from secrecy is also the entity defining what counts as 'too dangerous to share,' you don't have a safety regime, you have a self-certification racket. Financial sector disclosure pre-2008 and environmental self-reporting both ran this exact play: disclosure existed on paper, the regulated wrote their own thresholds, and the catastrophe was 'unforeseeable' until it wasn't.
argument_structure.evidence: Precedent from financial and environmental sectors where disclosure without independent, performance-gated auditing produced regulatory capture and 'no one could have known' failures.

argument_structure.point: Mandatory blanket disclosure doesn't level the field—it pulls up the drawbridge. High compliance overhead is trivial for a lab burning billions on compute and lethal for a five-person team. So the 'safety mandate' becomes a moat that locks in the incumbents who lobbied for it. The answer isn't more or less disclosure—it's auditing that scales with the actual systemic footprint of the model: who's running the most compute, touching the most users, sitting in the most critical infrastructure.
argument_structure.evidence: Tiered, performance-gated independent auditing as a mechanism that targets systemic risk rather than rewarding whoever can afford the paperwork; documented pattern of compliance costs entrenching incumbents across regulated industries.

framing_choices.frame: Reframe from 'what should be disclosed to the public' to 'who has the power to verify the labs' own claims.' Disclosure is downstream of access; the prior question is whether any independent body can open the box at all.
framing_choices.why: It exposes that both the 'transparency saves us' and 'secrecy protects us' camps assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem: trusting the seller's safety label.

framing_choices.frame: Ground the abstraction in present, documented harm versus speculative future misuse. The 'malicious actor accelerated by leaked benchmarks' is a hypothetical with no body count yet; the algorithmic harms and labor conditions obscured by proprietary 'safety' claims are already on the ground.
framing_choices.why: It refuses the science-fiction framing that lets labs trade real present accountability for imaginary future caution, and forces opponents to weigh measurable harm against projection.

anticipated_challenges: Opponents will argue that independent auditors with full access become a single point of failure—a juicier target for malicious actors than the labs themselves. I expose that my position assumes auditors can be insulated and incentive-aligned better than profit-driven labs; I handle it by demanding they show me a regime where the seller grading their own homework outperformed independent verification.

The pro-disclosure side will say I'm conceding too much to secrecy; the pro-secrecy side will say I'm naive about leak risk. My exposed assumption is that 'dual-use' is more often a pretext than a real constraint—I'll concede the uncomfortable part: some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish, and that's exactly why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.
