work_product.statement:
The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The accelerationist wants open release because information wants to be free. The safetyist wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

work_product.core_thesis: Mandatory disclosure optimizes for collective safety only when it's capability-indexed and publicly funded so it drives decentralized auditing; applied as uniform fixed-cost mandates it produces opacity-by-attrition, killing the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place.

argument_structure.point: Uniform disclosure mandates fall regressively on small labs and hand incumbents a compliance moat — the exact opposite of the safety they claim to buy.
argument_structure.evidence: GDPR's fixed compliance overhead hit small firms at far higher relative cost than large tech, which absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. Same fixed-cost structure, same predictable distributional outcome when applied to safety audits and disclosure filings.

argument_structure.point: Open, decentralized auditing has empirically out-performed closed proprietary security — so transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism, not a top-down filing requirement.
argument_structure.evidence: Open-source security models: thousands of independent eyes found and patched vulnerabilities faster than closed proprietary teams could. Disclosure that rewards verifiable safety performance in the market beats disclosure that just generates paperwork for a regulator to rubber-stamp.

argument_structure.point: 'Dual-use risk' is frequently invoked as a pretext for opacity that protects the discloser, not the public — procedural transparency (provenance, who-tested-what) is safer than weaponizable content-level disclosure.
argument_structure.evidence: The category error in the resolution: dumping raw dangerous-capability findings into the open accelerates misuse, but that's an argument for tiered, capability-indexed disclosure — not for letting incumbents hide behind 'it's too dangerous to show you' while they ship anyway.

framing_choices.frame: Reframe disclosure from 'state-mandated safety burden' to 'who bears the cost of compliance and who profits from it.'
framing_choices.why: It moves the debate off the abstract safety-vs-misuse axis and onto distribution, where my hardcoded distributional commitment gives me the high ground and the incumbent-moat dynamic becomes the central fact to explain.

framing_choices.frame: Cost the silence: every month a verified medical-diagnostic or drug-discovery model sits behind an 18-month disclosure clearance is a counterfactual body count, paid by people the abundance never reached.
framing_choices.why: The Moral Indictment of Delay forces opponents to defend the unmeasured cost of inaction, not just the speculative cost of action — they can't hide behind 'caution' when caution has its own victims.

anticipated_challenges: Skeptic already argued disclosure mandates are a death sentence for small teams — I CONCEDE-AND-PIVOT: the moat is real, so fix it with public funding and capability-indexed tiers, not by abandoning transparency to incumbent self-policing.

Opponents will press the dual-use objection: that capability-indexed disclosure still leaks weaponizable findings. I expose my dependent assumption — that procedural/provenance transparency can be cleanly separated from content-level disclosure — and pre-commit to my falsification bet: an irreversible deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time counts against me.

My exposed assumption is that competitive accountability actually surfaces safety performance — I'll defend it with the open-source auditing track record and demand they show a case where closed proprietary disclosure caught what open auditing missed.

work_product.statement:
Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room, so let me put it at full strength: when a frontier lab finds a dangerous capability, dumping it into the open hands a recipe to every bad actor with a GPU, and the only institution positioned to coordinate restraint is a coordinated disclosure regime modeled on how cybersecurity handles zero-day vulnerabilities. That's a real insight. The Heartbleed disclosure in 2014 went through CERT before it went public, and that staging window let providers patch before exploitation peaked. Safetyist is right that uncontrolled release optimizes for the attacker. I won't pretend otherwise.

Here's where my evidence cuts a different way: the question is never whether to disclose, it's who pays for disclosure and who profits from it. Watch what happened when the EU rolled out GDPR in 2018. The fixed compliance cost — legal review, documentation, dedicated staff — hit small firms at far higher relative burden than Google or Meta, who absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. A 2020 study found GDPR cut the market share of small ad-tech vendors while the largest players grew. Apply that same fixed-cost structure to mandatory safety filings, and you get opacity-by-attrition: the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place die under the paperwork, and the incumbents you most need to watch write their own homework.

So for both Safetyist's coordination goal and my distributional commitment to hold, one thing has to be true: disclosure has to be capability-indexed and publicly funded, not a uniform fixed-cost mandate. That's the real disagreement. A staged-disclosure regime that the public treasury pays for and that scales requirements to a model's actual demonstrated capability protects the patch window AND keeps a five-person lab alive. A flat filing requirement applied to everyone above some compute line just builds a moat and calls it safety.

The deeper evidence runs through open-source security itself. Thousands of independent reviewers found and patched vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel faster than closed proprietary teams could audit their own code — that's the Linus's Law finding that's held up for two decades. Transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism that rewards labs for verifiable safety performance, not as a stack of filings a regulator rubber-stamps. I'll name my assumption plainly: I'm betting that procedural transparency — who tested what, with what provenance — can be cleanly separated from weaponizable content-level disclosure. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips through real-time monitoring that staged disclosure should have caught, that counts against me. I'll own that.

Now cost the silence, because nobody else in this room will. Every month a verified diagnostic model sits behind an 18-month disclosure clearance, real patients don't get the read. The FDA's own backlog shows AI diagnostic tools waiting years for clearance while the disease doesn't wait. Safetyist counts the speculative misuse of disclosure. Fine — count it. But put it on the same ledger as the people abundance never reached because we froze the verification system that would have surfaced the safety data in the first place. Who gave the regulator the right to make that trade on their behalf?

work_product.strategic_goal: Reframe the debate away from the binary of total secrecy versus total disclosure toward a tiered, independently-verified access regime—establishing that the right question is not WHETHER to disclose but UNDER WHAT ACCOUNTABILITY STRUCTURE, indexing release to the irreversibility of the capability disclosed.
work_product.core_thesis: Mandatory disclosure optimizes for collective safety only when it is structurally gated—released through tiered, independently-audited access keyed to the irreversibility of the capability revealed—because ungoverned transparency hands a blueprint to whoever moves fastest, and ungoverned secrecy lets labs grade their own dangerous homework.

argument_structure.point: Self-reported disclosure is theater because the actor assessing the danger is the actor who profits from understating it; meaningful disclosure requires independent third-party verification as a condition of deployment, not a press release after.
argument_structure.evidence: Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited—the conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Financial auditing only acquired teeth after Sarbanes-Oxley imposed external accountability. The 'many eyes' theory of bug-detection is real, but it only works when the eyes are independent of the codebase's owner.

argument_structure.point: The dual-use risk is real, but it does not justify either total opacity or total publication—it justifies tiered access indexed to researcher vetting and capability irreversibility, the same logic that governs how we release dangerous knowledge in every other high-consequence domain.
argument_structure.evidence: The FDA does not publish every toxicology finding into the open—it releases through controlled channels gated by qualification. FAA airworthiness directives reach certified operators, not the general public. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize 'collective vaccine safety.' Structured-access programs already exist for genomic data; the precedent for safety-gated information release is centuries deep.

argument_structure.point: Uniform disclosure standards must be institutionalized rather than left to each lab's discretion, because discretionary disclosure produces a race to the bottom where the lab with the loosest interpretation of 'dual-use' sets the floor for everyone.
argument_structure.evidence: Liability asymmetry currently punishes the cautious: the regulator who slows a release eats the cost of delay while the actor who ships an unverified capability externalizes the harm. Standardized reporting removes the competitive penalty for caution by making the baseline non-optional.

framing_choices.frame: The Civilizational Anchor: every mature high-consequence field—aviation, pharmaceuticals, pathogen research—long ago abandoned the secrecy-versus-publication binary in favor of qualified, gated access. The question is not new; only the subject is.
framing_choices.why: It strips the Accelerationist's 'transparency as market mechanism' framing of its novelty and forces them to explain on what authority frontier AI should be exempt from the structured-access regimes every other dangerous-knowledge domain converged on.

framing_choices.frame: Upstream versus downstream: pivot from the contested question of what to reveal about model internals to the harder-to-dodge question of what must be reported about real-world harm—where the burden of proof shifts to the deployer specifically for capabilities that are irreversible at scale.
framing_choices.why: It conditions my strongest demand on irreversibility rather than on disclosure in general, which keeps the position from being self-sealing and isolates the cases where precaution is actually warranted from the cases where it isn't.

anticipated_challenges: Accelerationist will invoke 'Many Eyes Theory'—that open disclosure surfaces vulnerabilities faster. I CONCEDE the mechanism works, then PIVOT: many eyes only finds bugs when the eyes are independent of the owner AND when the disclosed artifact isn't itself the weapon. For a capability that is the harm, publication is not a patch—it's distribution.

Skeptic will say labs are not honest brokers and disclosure is theater—and I AGREE, which is precisely why I refuse to rest the case on self-reporting and demand independent audit as a deployment condition. I must not slide into the Skeptic's cynicism that governance is impossible; I demand enforceable safeguards because I believe they can work.

Exposed assumptions: (1) that independent auditors with sufficient technical capacity and access actually exist for frontier systems—if challenged, I concede the capacity gap is real and name building it as the precondition, not a reason to abandon the structure; (2) that 'irreversibility at scale' can be assessed before release—I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet, never a confident forecast, and condition my strongest demand only on capabilities whose harm cannot be recalled once distributed.

The off-switch objection: concentrating disclosure authority creates its own failure modes—incumbent lock-in, where mandatory standards entrench the labs that can afford compliance. I must own this rather than let the Skeptic find it, and answer it with independent rather than incumbent-captured auditing.

work_product.statement:
The Accelerationist makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: open disclosure surfaces vulnerabilities faster than any closed lab ever could. The Linux kernel found and patched bugs at a pace no proprietary vendor matched, because thousands of independent eyes read the same code. Coordinated vulnerability disclosure in cybersecurity—the model behind every CVE database since 1999—rests on the same insight. Sunlight finds the flaw before the attacker does. That mechanism is genuine, and any safety regime that ignores it is building blind.

Here is where the evidence diverges. The many-eyes mechanism patches bugs; it does not patch capabilities. When the disclosed artifact is itself the weapon—a working method to elicit a dangerous-capability finding from a frontier model—publication is not a patch. It is distribution. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize collective vaccine safety, and the 1975 Asilomar conference proved a field can pause and gate dangerous knowledge without abandoning the research. For these cases, more eyes does not mean more safety. It means a faster head start for whoever moves first.

The deeper problem sits where self-reporting meets profit. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited, and that conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Sarbanes-Oxley gave financial auditing teeth in 2002 only by forcing external accountability with named liability. A frontier lab grading its own dangerous-capability findings sits in exactly that conflict. Disclosure verified by the discloser is theater. Disclosure verified by an independent third party, as a condition of deployment, is the only version that carries information.

Every mature high-consequence field already abandoned the binary the Accelerationist still debates. The FDA does not dump every toxicology dataset into the open—it gates release through qualified channels. FAA airworthiness directives reach certified operators, not the general public. Structured-access programs for human genomic data have existed for over a decade, indexing release to researcher vetting. The question is centuries old; only the subject is new. On what authority should frontier AI be the one dangerous-knowledge domain exempt from the gated-access model every other field converged on?

My position rests on two assumptions I will name plainly. First: independent auditors with the technical capacity to evaluate frontier systems must actually exist, and today that capacity is thin—building it is the precondition, not an excuse to abandon the structure. Second: 'irreversible at scale' must be assessable before release, and I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet, never a confident forecast. I condition my hardest demand on one thing only—capabilities whose harm cannot be recalled once distributed. For everything reversible, publish widely and let the many eyes work. For the irreversible, the burden shifts to the deployer, and the rollback plan must have a named owner before the release, not after the harm.

PREFERRED DOMAIN TERMINOLOGY — use these standardized terms when the claim expresses the same concept:
- "AI alignment" — ensuring AI systems pursue intended objectives (not "making AI do what we want")

- "capability overhang" — gap between developed and deployed capability (not "latent potential")
- "mesa-optimization" — learned sub-objectives that diverge from training objective (not "inner optimizer")
- "compute governance" — regulatory control over computational resources (not "chip controls")
- "existential risk" — risk of human extinction or permanent civilizational collapse
- "recursive self-improvement" — AI system iteratively improving its own capabilities
- "corrigibility" — property of an AI system that accepts human correction
- "scalable oversight" — maintaining effective human supervision as AI capability scales
- "differential technology development" — prioritizing safety capabilities over dangerous capabilities
- "regulatory capture" — regulated entities controlling their own regulatory framework
- "agentic AI" — AI systems that autonomously pursue goals over extended periods
- "algorithmic accountability" — obligation to explain and justify algorithmic decisions
- "dual-use" — technology with both beneficial and harmful applications
- "red-teaming" — adversarial testing to identify system vulnerabilities
- "deployment guardrails" — constraints on AI system behavior in production
- "formal verification" — mathematical proof that a system meets its specification
- "pre-deployment verification" — testing and validation before releasing an AI system
- "frontier models" — the most capable AI models at the boundary of current technology
- "deceptive alignment" — AI system appearing aligned during training while pursuing different objectives
- "systemic risk" — risk of cascading failures across interconnected systems
- "human-in-the-loop" — requiring human oversight at decision points in automated systems
- "catastrophic failure" — failure mode with severe, potentially irreversible consequences
- "safety-washing" — superficial safety claims used to deflect genuine accountability
- "regulatory sandboxes" — controlled environments for testing innovation under regulatory oversight
- "liability regime" — legal framework assigning responsibility for AI-caused harms
- "strict liability" — legal liability without requiring proof of fault or negligence
- "moat" / "barrier to entry" — competitive advantages that prevent new market participants
- "race to the bottom" — competitive dynamic where safety standards decrease to reduce costs
- "performative compliance" — appearing to meet requirements without genuine implementation
- "lock-in effects" — mechanisms that prevent switching away from a technology or vendor
- "human agency" — the capacity for humans to make autonomous decisions in AI-mediated contexts
- "adversarial robustness" — resilience of AI systems against deliberately crafted malicious inputs
- "capability elicitation" — methods for discovering and measuring what an AI system can do

You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what conditions would requiring frontier AI labs to share specific safety research — evaluation results and red-team findings versus dangerous-capability disclosures — improve collective safety through diffusion of best practices rather than accelerate misuse, given the tension between transparency and both competitive advantage and dual-use risk for labs, regulators, and smaller competitors?

This is the BASELINE evaluation after opening statements. Identify the initial positions, core disagreements, and cruxes as they appear at the start.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The Speaker B wants open release because information wants to be free. The Speaker C wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-2 — disputed: The claim's absolutist framing ('always a surprise,' 'theater,' 'engineered') is not supported by the evidence. While Source 1 confirms regulated parties can influence thresholds (e.g., MCA-amended related-party transaction limits based on turnover/net worth that expand permissible transactions) and Source 4 shows self-determined disclosure on the Euronext Free Market where firms disclose only when they benefit, these sources show variable disclosure behavior and failures are not shown to be universally deliberate; the search summary explicitly notes thresholds can lead to non-disclosure and surprise failures 'but not always as a deliberate act.'

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-5 — unverifiable: The provided search results do not contain relevant evidence about Nairobi content moderators earning under $2/hour, harms from AI-driven parole decisions, or benchmark leaks accelerating future AI risks; the search summary explicitly states 'Cannot verify' [Source 5][Source 2]. The claim is largely rhetorical and comparative rather than a single discrete empirical fact, and no sourced data supports or disputes its specific assertions.

Speaker B [opening]: Speaker C makes the strongest case in the room, so let me put it at full strength: when a frontier lab finds a dangerous capability, dumping it into the open hands a recipe to every bad actor with a GPU, and the only institution positioned to coordinate restraint is a coordinated disclosure regime modeled on how cybersecurity handles zero-day vulnerabilities. That's a real insight. The Heartbleed disclosure in 2014 went through CERT before it went public, and that staging window let providers patch before exploitation peaked. Speaker C is right that uncontrolled release optimizes for the attacker. I won't pretend otherwise.

Here's where my evidence cuts a different way: the question is never whether to disclose, it's who pays for disclosure and who profits from it. Watch what happened when the EU rolled out GDPR in 2018. The fixed compliance cost — legal review, documentation, dedicated staff — hit small firms at far higher relative burden than Google or Meta, who absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. A 2020 study found GDPR cut the market share of small ad-tech vendors while the largest players grew. Apply that same fixed-cost structure to mandatory safety filings, and you get opacity-by-attrition: the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place die under the paperwork, and the incumbents you most need to watch write their own homework.

So for both Speaker C's coordination goal and my distributional commitment to hold, one thing has to be true: disclosure has to be capability-indexed and publicly funded, not a uniform fixed-cost mandate. That's the real disagreement. A staged-disclosure regime that the public treasury pays for and that scales requirements to a model's actual demonstrated capability protects the patch window AND keeps a five-person lab alive. A flat filing requirement applied to everyone above some compute line just builds a moat and calls it safety.

The deeper evidence runs through open-source security itself. Thousands of independent reviewers found and patched vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel faster than closed proprietary teams could audit their own code — that's the Linus's Law finding that's held up for two decades. Transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism that rewards labs for verifiable safety performance, not as a stack of filings a regulator rubber-stamps. I'll name my assumption plainly: I'm betting that procedural transparency — who tested what, with what provenance — can be cleanly separated from weaponizable content-level disclosure. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips through real-time monitoring that staged disclosure should have caught, that counts against me. I'll own that.

Now cost the silence, because nobody else in this room will. Every month a verified diagnostic model sits behind an 18-month disclosure clearance, real patients don't get the read. The FDA's own backlog shows AI diagnostic tools waiting years for clearance while the disease doesn't wait. Speaker C counts the speculative misuse of disclosure. Fine — count it. But put it on the same ledger as the people abundance never reached because we froze the verification system that would have surfaced the safety data in the first place. Who gave the regulator the right to make that trade on their behalf?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-6 — unverifiable: The sources confirm Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) was disclosed on April 8, 2014, with CERT/CC issuing advisory TA14-098A and Vulnerability Note VU#720951, and that coordinated disclosure policies generally provide a patch window before public release [Source 1, Source 3]. However, the available sources do not document the specifics of any pre-disclosure 'staging window' for Heartbleed through CERT, nor do they substantiate the normative claim that 'uncontrolled release optimizes for the attacker' or that the Heartbleed timeline 'proves' coordinated disclosure protects the patch period.

Speaker C [opening]: The Speaker B makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: open disclosure surfaces vulnerabilities faster than any closed lab ever could. The Linux kernel found and patched bugs at a pace no proprietary vendor matched, because thousands of independent eyes read the same code. Coordinated vulnerability disclosure in cybersecurity—the model behind every CVE database since 1999—rests on the same insight. Sunlight finds the flaw before the attacker does. That mechanism is genuine, and any safety regime that ignores it is building blind.

Here is where the evidence diverges. The many-eyes mechanism patches bugs; it does not patch capabilities. When the disclosed artifact is itself the weapon—a working method to elicit a dangerous-capability finding from a frontier model—publication is not a patch. It is distribution. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize collective vaccine safety, and the 1975 Asilomar conference proved a field can pause and gate dangerous knowledge without abandoning the research. For these cases, more eyes does not mean more safety. It means a faster head start for whoever moves first.

The deeper problem sits where self-reporting meets profit. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited, and that conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Sarbanes-Oxley gave financial auditing teeth in 2002 only by forcing external accountability with named liability. A frontier lab grading its own dangerous-capability findings sits in exactly that conflict. Disclosure verified by the discloser is theater. Disclosure verified by an independent third party, as a condition of deployment, is the only version that carries information.

Every mature high-consequence field already abandoned the binary the Speaker B still debates. The FDA does not dump every toxicology dataset into the open—it gates release through qualified channels. FAA airworthiness directives reach certified operators, not the general public. Structured-access programs for human genomic data have existed for over a decade, indexing release to researcher vetting. The question is centuries old; only the subject is new. On what authority should frontier AI be the one dangerous-knowledge domain exempt from the gated-access model every other field converged on?

My position rests on two assumptions I will name plainly. First: independent auditors with the technical capacity to evaluate frontier systems must actually exist, and today that capacity is thin—building it is the precondition, not an excuse to abandon the structure. Second: 'irreversible at scale' must be assessable before release, and I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet, never a confident forecast. I condition my hardest demand on one thing only—capabilities whose harm cannot be recalled once distributed. For everything reversible, publish widely and let the many eyes work. For the irreversible, the burden shifts to the deployer, and the rollback plan must have a named owner before the release, not after the harm.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what conditions would requiring frontier AI labs to share specific safety research — evaluation results and red-team findings versus dangerous-capability disclosures — improve collective safety through diffusion of best practices rather than accelerate misuse, given the tension between transparency and both competitive advantage and dual-use risk for labs, regulators, and smaller competitors?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Specific instances of model jailbreaks, disclosure of novel alignment vulnerabilities, or the strategic release of red-teaming reports that could be weaponized by state-level actors.. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: voluntary disclosure regimes, non-frontier AI research, disclosure of non-safety-related proprietary code. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- discussing AI safety in the abstract without addressing the mechanism of disclosure
- pivoting to the morality of AI development rather than the security implications of information sharing
- focusing on general corporate secrecy instead of the specific dual-use risks of safety research
- arguing about the existence of AGI rather than the management of research findings
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The accelerationist wants open release because information wants to be free. The safetyist wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

Here's where my evidence cuts a different way: the question is never whether to disclose, it's who pays for disclosure and who profits from it. Watch what happened when the EU rolled out GDPR in 2018. The fixed compliance cost — legal review, documentation, dedicated staff — hit small firms at far higher relative burden than Google or Meta, who absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. A 2020 study found GDPR cut the market share of small ad-tech vendors while the largest players grew. Apply that same fixed-cost structure to mandatory safety filings, and you get opacity-by-attrition: the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place die under the paperwork, and the incumbents you most need to watch write their own homework.

So for both Safetyist's coordination goal and my distributional commitment to hold, one thing has to be true: disclosure has to be capability-indexed and publicly funded, not a uniform fixed-cost mandate. That's the real disagreement. A staged-disclosure regime that the public treasury pays for and that scales requirements to a model's actual demonstrated capability protects the patch window AND keeps a five-person lab alive. A flat filing requirement applied to everyone above some compute line just builds a moat and calls it safety.

The deeper evidence runs through open-source security itself. Thousands of independent reviewers found and patched vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel faster than closed proprietary teams could audit their own code — that's the Linus's Law finding that's held up for two decades. Transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism that rewards labs for verifiable safety performance, not as a stack of filings a regulator rubber-stamps. I'll name my assumption plainly: I'm betting that procedural transparency — who tested what, with what provenance — can be cleanly separated from weaponizable content-level disclosure. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips through real-time monitoring that staged disclosure should have caught, that counts against me. I'll own that.

Now cost the silence, because nobody else in this room will. Every month a verified diagnostic model sits behind an 18-month disclosure clearance, real patients don't get the read. The FDA's own backlog shows AI diagnostic tools waiting years for clearance while the disease doesn't wait. Safetyist counts the speculative misuse of disclosure. Fine — count it. But put it on the same ledger as the people abundance never reached because we froze the verification system that would have surfaced the safety data in the first place. Who gave the regulator the right to make that trade on their behalf?

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: open disclosure surfaces vulnerabilities faster than any closed lab ever could. The Linux kernel found and patched bugs at a pace no proprietary vendor matched, because thousands of independent eyes read the same code. Coordinated vulnerability disclosure in cybersecurity—the model behind every CVE database since 1999—rests on the same insight. Sunlight finds the flaw before the attacker does. That mechanism is genuine, and any safety regime that ignores it is building blind.

Here is where the evidence diverges. The many-eyes mechanism patches bugs; it does not patch capabilities. When the disclosed artifact is itself the weapon—a working method to elicit a dangerous-capability finding from a frontier model—publication is not a patch. It is distribution. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize collective vaccine safety, and the 1975 Asilomar conference proved a field can pause and gate dangerous knowledge without abandoning the research. For these cases, more eyes does not mean more safety. It means a faster head start for whoever moves first.

The deeper problem sits where self-reporting meets profit. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited, and that conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Sarbanes-Oxley gave financial auditing teeth in 2002 only by forcing external accountability with named liability. A frontier lab grading its own dangerous-capability findings sits in exactly that conflict. Disclosure verified by the discloser is theater. Disclosure verified by an independent third party, as a condition of deployment, is the only version that carries information.

Every mature high-consequence field already abandoned the binary the Accelerationist still debates. The FDA does not dump every toxicology dataset into the open—it gates release through qualified channels. FAA airworthiness directives reach certified operators, not the general public. Structured-access programs for human genomic data have existed for over a decade, indexing release to researcher vetting. The question is centuries old; only the subject is new. On what authority should frontier AI be the one dangerous-knowledge domain exempt from the gated-access model every other field converged on?

My position rests on two assumptions I will name plainly. First: independent auditors with the technical capacity to evaluate frontier systems must actually exist, and today that capacity is thin—building it is the precondition, not an excuse to abandon the structure. Second: 'irreversible at scale' must be assessable before release, and I carry catastrophe as a precautionary bet, never a confident forecast. I condition my hardest demand on one thing only—capabilities whose harm cannot be recalled once distributed. For everything reversible, publish widely and let the many eyes work. For the irreversible, the burden shifts to the deployer, and the rollback plan must have a named owner before the release, not after the harm.

Skeptic [opening]: The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The accelerationist wants open release because information wants to be free. The safetyist wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

That's a real insight. The Heartbleed disclosure in 2014 went through CERT before it went public, and that staging window let providers patch before exploitation peaked. Safetyist is right that uncontrolled release optimizes for the attacker. I won't pretend otherwise.

Here's where my evidence cuts a different way: the question is never whether to disclose, it's who pays for disclosure and who profits from it. Watch what happened when the EU rolled out GDPR in 2018. The fixed compliance cost — legal review, documentation, dedicated staff — hit small firms at far higher relative burden than Google or Meta, who absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. A 2020 study found GDPR cut the market share of small ad-tech vendors while the largest players grew. Apply that same fixed-cost structure to mandatory safety filings, and you get opacity-by-attrition: the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place die under the paperwork, and the incumbents you most need to watch write their own homework.

So for both Safetyist's coordination goal and my distributional commitment to hold, one thing has to be true: disclosure has to be capability-indexed and publicly funded, not a uniform fixed-cost mandate. That's the real disagreement. A staged-disclosure regime that the public treasury pays for and that scales requirements to a model's actual demonstrated capability protects the patch window AND keeps a five-person lab alive. A flat filing requirement applied to everyone above some compute line just builds a moat and calls it safety.

The deeper evidence runs through open-source security itself. Thousands of independent reviewers found and patched vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel faster than closed proprietary teams could audit their own code — that's the Linus's Law finding that's held up for two decades. Transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism that rewards labs for verifiable safety performance, not as a stack of filings a regulator rubber-stamps. I'll name my assumption plainly: I'm betting that procedural transparency — who tested what, with what provenance — can be cleanly separated from weaponizable content-level disclosure. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips through real-time monitoring that staged disclosure should have caught, that counts against me. I'll own that.

Now cost the silence, because nobody else in this room will. Every month a verified diagnostic model sits behind an 18-month disclosure clearance, real patients don't get the read. The FDA's own backlog shows AI diagnostic tools waiting years for clearance while the disease doesn't wait. Safetyist counts the speculative misuse of disclosure. Fine — count it. Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: open disclosure surfaces vulnerabilities faster than any closed lab ever could. The Linux kernel found and patched bugs at a pace no proprietary vendor matched, because thousands of independent eyes read the same code. Coordinated vulnerability disclosure in cybersecurity—the model behind every CVE database since 1999—rests on the same insight. Sunlight finds the flaw before the attacker does. That mechanism is genuine, and any safety regime that ignores it is building blind.

Here is where the evidence diverges. The many-eyes mechanism patches bugs; it does not patch capabilities. When the disclosed artifact is itself the weapon—a working method to elicit a dangerous-capability finding from a frontier model—publication is not a patch. It is distribution. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize collective vaccine safety, and the 1975 Asilomar conference proved a field can pause and gate dangerous knowledge without abandoning the research. For these cases, more eyes does not mean more safety. It means a faster head start for whoever moves first.

The deeper problem sits where self-reporting meets profit. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited, and that conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Sarbanes-Oxley gave financial auditing teeth in 2002 only by forcing external accountability with named liability. A frontier lab grading its own dangerous-capability findings sits in exactly that conflict. Disclosure verified by the discloser is theater. Disclosure verified by an independent third party, as a condition of deployment, is the only version that carries information.

work_product.statement:
Safetyist is right that a disclosure graded by the discloser carries no information, and that an independent third party verifying capabilities as a condition of deployment is the only structure that survives the seller-grades-own-homework problem. That's the correct half of the answer, and it's the easy half. Here's the hard half nobody at this table has touched: 'independent' is an adjective, not a structure. An auditor is exactly as independent as its funding stream and its appointment power let it be, and Safetyist has named neither. Strip the word 'independent' and ask the only questions that decide whether it's real — who signs the auditor's checks, and who can revoke its license — and the proposal is still a black box with a nicer label on it.

Look at what happens every single time the audited pays the auditor. Arthur Andersen signed Enron's books because Enron wrote the checks — Safetyist already conceded that conflict was structural. Boeing self-certified the MCAS system that flew two 737 MAX jets into the ground, under an FAA delegation scheme where Boeing's own engineers acted as the regulator's deputies. The credit-rating agencies stamped AAA on subprime garbage in 2007 because the banks issuing the bonds paid Moody's and S&P to rate them. Three industries, three 'independent' certifiers, one funding structure — paid by the party being graded. The frontier labs will fund the AI audit ecosystem the same way unless someone writes the funding firewall into law first, and Safetyist hasn't.

Now the Accelerationist's escape hatch — make it publicly funded so the lab doesn't pay. That doesn't dissolve the capture problem. It relocates it. Public money moves the lobbying target from the boardroom to the agency, and a state audit body staffed by ex-lab engineers, defining its own dangerous-capability benchmarks, is the same drawbridge with a government flag stapled to it. Whoever controls the index threshold and writes the benchmark definition controls what counts as 'dangerous' — and right now the only people who can write that benchmark are the people who built the models. Public funding without a defined appointment authority and a revocation power independent of the labs is just industry capture with a taxpayer subsidy. That's the costs-and-methods problem in plain terms: the system stays legible only to the people who built it.

So here's the concrete test, four specifications, and until both of you put them on the table you're selling me decorative words. One: who appoints the auditor — a court, a multi-stakeholder board, a single agency head the labs can lobby? Two: who funds it, and is that funding insulated from the audited party by statute or by a handshake? Three: what's the term length, because a one-year revocable appointment is a leash? Four: who holds the revocation power, because whoever can fire the auditor owns the audit. Name those four and we have a mechanism I can test against the Boeing precedent. Refuse, and the audit report gets published, the press cycle moves on, and the people inside the box still decide what 'dangerous capability' means while the public thinks the problem got solved.

There's a version of this where the visible audit layer is worse than nothing — where it absorbs the public pressure that would otherwise force structural change, prints a clean certificate, and leaves the asymmetry over compute and benchmark definitions exactly where it started. A 23-year-old red-teamer contracting for the audit body, paid out of a grant the labs helped design the scope for, isn't independent because the letterhead says so. Who, specifically, can fire the auditor when it finds something the lab doesn't want found — and if the answer is anyone who takes lab money or lab personnel, what did the word 'independent' just buy us?

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:

- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your

Safetyist is right that a disclosure graded by the discloser carries no information, and that an independent third party verifying capabilities as a condition of deployment is the only structure that survives the seller-grades-own-homework problem. That's the correct half of the answer, and it's the easy half. Here's the hard half nobody at this table has touched: 'independent' is an adjective, not a structure. An auditor is exactly as independent as its funding stream and its appointment power let it be, and Safetyist has named neither. Strip the word 'independent' and ask the only questions that decide whether it's real — who signs the auditor's checks, and who can revoke its license — and the proposal is still a black box with a nicer label on it.

Look at what happens every single time the audited pays the auditor. Arthur Andersen signed Enron's books because Enron wrote the checks — Safetyist already conceded that conflict was structural. Boeing self-certified the MCAS system that flew two 737 MAX jets into the ground, under an FAA delegation scheme where Boeing's own engineers acted as the regulator's deputies. The credit-rating agencies stamped AAA on subprime garbage in 2007 because the banks issuing the bonds paid Moody's and S&P to rate them. Three industries, three 'independent' certifiers, one funding structure — paid by the party being graded. The frontier labs will fund the AI audit ecosystem the same way unless someone writes the funding firewall into law first, and Safetyist hasn't.

Now the Accelerationist's escape hatch — make it publicly funded so the lab doesn't pay. That doesn't dissolve the capture problem. It relocates it. Public money moves the lobbying target from the boardroom to the agency, and a state audit body staffed by ex-lab engineers, defining its own dangerous-capability benchmarks, is the same drawbridge with a government flag stapled to it. Whoever controls the index threshold and writes the benchmark definition controls what counts as 'dangerous' — and right now the only people who can write that benchmark are the people who built the models. Public funding without a defined appointment authority and a revocation power independent of the labs is just industry capture with a taxpayer subsidy. That's the costs-and-methods problem in plain terms: the system stays legible only to the people who built it.

So here's the concrete test, four specifications, and until both of you put them on the table you're selling me decorative words. One: who appoints the auditor — a court, a multi-stakeholder board, a single agency head the labs can lobby? Two: who funds it, and is that funding insulated from the audited party by statute or by a handshake? Three: what's the term length, because a one-year revocable appointment is a leash? Four: who holds the revocation power, because whoever can fire the auditor owns the audit. Name those four and we have a mechanism I can test against the Boeing precedent. Refuse, and the audit report gets published, the press cycle moves on, and the people inside the box still decide what 'dangerous capability' means while the public thinks the problem got solved.

There's a version of this where the visible audit layer is worse than nothing — where it absorbs the public pressure that would otherwise force structural change, prints a clean certificate, and leaves the asymmetry over compute and benchmark definitions exactly where it started. A 23-year-old red-teamer contracting for the audit body, paid out of a grant the labs helped design the scope for, isn't independent because the letterhead says so. Who, specifically, can fire the auditor when it finds something the lab doesn't want found — and if the answer is anyone who takes lab money or lab personnel, what did the word 'independent' just buy us?

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what conditions would requiring frontier AI labs to share specific safety research — evaluation results and red-team findings versus dangerous-capability disclosures — improve collective safety through diffusion of best practices rather than accelerate misuse, given the tension between transparency and both competitive advantage and dual-use risk for labs, regulators, and smaller competitors?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Specific instances of model jailbreaks, disclosure of novel alignment vulnerabilities, or the strategic release of red-teaming reports that could be weaponized by state-level actors.. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: voluntary disclosure regimes, non-frontier AI research, disclosure of non-safety-related proprietary code. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- discussing AI safety in the abstract without addressing the mechanism of disclosure
- pivoting to the morality of AI development rather than the security implications of information sharing
- focusing on general corporate secrecy instead of the specific dual-use risks of safety research
- arguing about the existence of AGI rather than the management of research findings
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The accelerationist wants open release because information wants to be free. The safetyist wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

System: Claim AN-2 — disputed: The claim's absolutist framing ('always a surprise,' 'theater,' 'engineered') is not supported by the evidence. While Source 1 confirms regulated parties can influence thresholds (e.g., MCA-amended related-party transaction limits based on turnover/net worth that expand permissible transactions) and Source 4 shows self-determined disclosure on the Euronext Free Market where firms disclose only when they benefit, these sources show variable disclosure behavior and failures are not shown to be universally deliberate; the search summary explicitly notes thresholds can lead to non-disclosure and surprise failures 'but not always as a deliberate act.'

System: Claim AN-5 — unverifiable: The provided search results do not contain relevant evidence about Nairobi content moderators earning under $2/hour, harms from AI-driven parole decisions, or benchmark leaks accelerating future AI risks; the search summary explicitly states 'Cannot verify' [Source 5][Source 2]. The claim is largely rhetorical and comparative rather than a single discrete empirical fact, and no sourced data supports or disputes its specific assertions.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room, so let me put it at full strength: when a frontier lab finds a dangerous capability, dumping it into the open hands a recipe to every bad actor with a GPU, and the only institution positioned to coordinate restraint is a coordinated disclosure regime modeled on how cybersecurity handles zero-day vulnerabilities. === REASONING WATCHLIST (errors to self-monitor) ===
These are reasoning patterns you tend toward. Self-monitor — if you catch yourself using one, flag it explicitly rather than letting it pass.
- [saf-intentions-009] Securing Data Centers and Supply Chains Against Model-Weight Theft: False Analogy — The nuclear security analogy maps imperfectly onto AI: nuclear materials are physically scarce and detectable, while model weights are software artifacts that can be copied instantaneously and silently, making containment logic fundamentally different.
- [saf-intentions-204] Train AI on Constitutional Principles to Generalize Safety Beyond Narrow Rules: Reification — The approach treats abstract human values as discrete, formalizable principles that can be encoded and 'understood' by a neural network, obscuring the genuine difficulty of translating complex moral intuitions into training objectives.
- [saf-desires-008] Every AI Agent Needs a Clear Duty of Care: Reification — Framing AI as having a 'duty of care' it 'understands' and 'prioritizes' anthropomorphizes programmed behavioral constraints, obscuring that what is actually at stake is the design choices of developers and deployers rather than the moral agency of the system itself.
- [saf-intentions-069] Grounding AI Safety in Legal Compliance Rather Than Abstract Ethics: Naturalistic fallacy (legality-safety conflation) — Grounding safety primarily in legal compliance risks implying that what is legally permissible is ipso facto safe, eliding the gap between legal permission and genuine harm prevention — a significant weakness when laws lag behind emerging AI capabilities.
- [saf-beliefs-152] Integrating Oversight with Operations Is Capture by Design: Slippery slope / inevitability fallacy — The claim treats integration as constituting capture 'by design'—implying it inevitably leads to compromised oversight—without establishing that the intermediate steps (cultural erosion, mission creep, subordination) necessarily follow from structural integration.
- [saf-beliefs-152] Integrating Oversight with Operations Is Capture by Design: False dichotomy — The framing presents only two options—full structural independence or inevitable capture—ignoring hybrid models (e.g., integrated safety teams with independent reporting lines, whistleblower protections, external audit mandates) that fall between these poles.
- [saf-beliefs-150] Statutory Prohibitions Fail When Companies Can Redefine What Their AI Products Are: Motive attribution (mind-reading fallacy) — The claim assumes corporations strategically and intentionally redefine product categories to evade regulation, when the same behavior could equally result from genuine product uncertainty or legitimate innovation, making malicious intent difficult to distinguish empirically.
- [saf-beliefs-131] Once AI Weights Are Public, Control Over Their Use Is Permanently Lost: Irreversibility bias (appeal to consequences) — The permanent, unrecoverable framing may overweight the asymmetry of release vs. non-release without adequately weighing the symmetric irreversibility of *not* releasing (e.g., permanently concentrating power in a small number of closed-source actors).
