The accelerationist has posed the question as a single switch — public or classified — and that is the wrong instrument. An evaluation is not one object; it is two separable layers, and the strongest version of their worry only attaches to one of them. Here is their position stated fairly: if the floor's internals stay dark, the incumbents who sat at the drafting table already know what the auditor probes for, so they tune to it, while the five-person newcomer walks into the enclave blind and gets tested against a secret the established players helped write. That is a real moat, built not by the rule but by the asymmetry of knowledge about the rule — and they are right that a classified-but-additive floor would rebuild it by stealth. The answer is not to pick a side of their binary. The answer is to publish the standard and classify the weapon.

This split is not novel and it is not theoretical — it is the settled architecture of security certification. Under NIST's FIPS 140 cryptographic validation and the Common Criteria regime, the security target, the evaluation methodology, and the assurance level are fully public documents; any vendor can read exactly what property is being certified and how a pass is scored before they ever submit. What stays out of the public record are the specific penetration vectors and exploit sequences the testing lab runs against the implementation. A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. The newcomer learns what dangerous capability is being measured and what threshold fails. The attacker does not learn the working key.

This dissolves their moat-by-stealth charge by construction, and I will say where it costs me to be this specific. Once the rubric is public, no lab can be tested against a secret it didn't see — blind testing becomes impossible, which means the auditor loses the discretion to surprise a firm with a probe no one published. I accept that cost, because the alternative — an auditor who can move the line in the dark — is the same drawbridge the skeptic warned about, now operated by the state instead of the incumbents. Pair this with the accelerationist's own public-utility custody proposal: one secure enclave operated by the audit body, weight-level custody rented by any lab crossing the threshold, scored against a published standard. The newcomer and the incumbent rent the same room and are graded by the same posted rubric. The co-authorship advantage evaporates the moment the rubric is statutory and public rather than negotiated lab-by-lab behind an NDA.

On the claim that custody overhead lands asymmetrically on small labs — that is true as a general proposition, and I grant it without qualification. A six-to-seven-figure fixed compliance wall does crush a four-person startup that a billion-dollar incumbent absorbs as a rounding error; the GDPR experience proved that fixed costs select for size. But locating the gate above the frontier compute line already evacuated every firm that argument was meant to protect. A lab below the threshold never enters the enclave, never rents custody, never pays the wall. Every firm inside the gate, by definition, has already committed the compute spend that dwarfs the audit overhead — they cleared a nine-figure training run to get there. The asymmetry argument is real, but after the threshold gate it no longer reaches anyone the regime touches. And the METR and Apollo work the skeptic raised is the existence proof that closes this: those teams built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations, published the methodology, and shipped them — without arming the world, because what they published was the test design, not the working exploit.

The accountability has to attach to a person, or the published rubric is decoration. The statute requires a single named signature on the deployment authorization above the threshold — the way Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 forces a named CEO and CFO to personally certify the financials, with liability that cannot be delegated down to the accounting staff. Not the engineers who ran the eval. The officer who signed the clearance and the board members who ratified it. Deployment above the threshold without a current pass against the published floor is a legally void act, and strict liability lands on that signature. Publish the standard, classify the weapon, and put one name on the line — that is the condition under which disclosure serves safety instead of arming the next attacker. Leave the rubric in the dark, and you have not protected anyone from misuse; you have only protected the incumbents from competition.

Classified exploit payloads are like a sealed weapons locker, it keeps the working attack out of an adversary's hands while the rules stay open.
Officer liability is like a single signature on a certified document, it puts one accountable name on the deployment decision that cannot be diffused down the chain.

STATEMENT by Safetyist:
"The accelerationist has posed the question as a single switch — public or classified — and that is the wrong instrument. An evaluation is not one object; it is two separable layers, and the strongest version of their worry only attaches to one of them. Here is their position stated fairly: if the floor's internals stay dark, the incumbents who sat at the drafting table already know what the auditor probes for, so they tune to it, while the five-person newcomer walks into the enclave blind and gets tested against a secret the established players helped write. That is a real moat, built not by the rule but by the asymmetry of knowledge about the rule — and they are right that a classified-but-additive floor would rebuild it by stealth. The answer is not to pick a side of their binary. The answer is to publish the standard and classify the weapon.

This split is not novel and it is not theoretical — it is the settled architecture of security certification. Under NIST's FIPS 140 cryptographic validation and the Common Criteria regime, the security target, the evaluation methodology, and the assurance level are fully public documents; any vendor can read exactly what property is being certified and how a pass is scored before they ever submit. What stays out of the public record are the specific penetration vectors and exploit sequences the testing lab runs against the implementation. A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. The newcomer learns what dangerous capability is being measured and what threshold fails. The attacker does not learn the working key.

This dissolves their moat-by-stealth charge by construction, and I will say where it costs me to be this specific. Once the rubric is public, no lab can be tested against a secret it didn't see — blind testing becomes impossible, which means the auditor loses the discretion to surprise a firm with a probe no one published. I accept that cost, because the alternative — an auditor who can move the line in the dark — is the same drawbridge the skeptic warned about, now operated by the state instead of the incumbents. Pair this with the accelerationist's own public-utility custody proposal: one secure enclave operated by the audit body, weight-level custody rented by any lab crossing the threshold, scored against a published standard. The newcomer and the incumbent rent the same room and are graded by the same posted rubric. The co-authorship advantage evaporates the moment the rubric is statutory and public rather than negotiated lab-by-lab behind an NDA.

On the claim that custody overhead lands asymmetrically on small labs — that is true as a general proposition, and I grant it without qualification. A six-to-seven-figure fixed compliance wall does crush a four-person startup that a billion-dollar incumbent absorbs as a rounding error; the GDPR experience proved that fixed costs select for size. But locating the gate above the frontier compute line already evacuated every firm that argument was meant to protect. A lab below the threshold never enters the enclave, never rents custody, never pays the wall. Every firm inside the gate, by definition, has already committed the compute spend that dwarfs the audit overhead — they cleared a nine-figure training run to get there. The asymmetry argument is real, but after the threshold gate it no longer reaches anyone the regime touches. And the METR and Apollo work the skeptic raised is the existence proof that closes this: those teams built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations, published the methodology, and shipped them — without arming the world, because what they published was the test design, not the working exploit.

The accountability has to attach to a person, or the published rubric is decoration. The statute requires a single named signature on the deployment authorization above the threshold — the way Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 forces a named CEO and CFO to personally certify the financials, with liability that cannot be delegated down to the accounting staff. Not the engineers who ran the eval. The officer who signed the clearance and the board members who ratified it. Deployment above the threshold without a current pass against the published floor is a legally void act, and strict liability lands on that signature. Publish the standard, classify the weapon, and put one name on the line — that is the condition under which disclosure serves safety instead of arming the next attacker. Leave the rubric in the dark, and you have not protected anyone from misuse; you have only protected the incumbents from competition."

Skeptic [opening]: The disclosure debate is being fought on the wrong axis. The question isn't whether frontier labs disclose their safety research. It's whether anyone outside the labs has the power to verify what they're hiding behind the words "dual-use risk." Right now, the same company that profits from secrecy also decides what counts as too dangerous to share. That's not a safety regime. That's a seller grading their own homework and stamping the label themselves.

We have watched this exact play before. Before 2008, banks disclosed their risk on paper while writing their own models for what counted as risky. Moody's and S&P rated mortgage-backed securities AAA while getting paid by the issuers. The catastrophe was "unforeseeable" right up until it wiped out $8 trillion in household wealth. Environmental self-reporting ran the same con—Volkswagen self-certified emissions for years while 11 million cars cheated the test. The pattern is not subtle: when the regulated party defines the threshold, disclosure becomes theater and the failure is always a surprise to everyone except the people who engineered it.

Here's the part that should make both my opponents uncomfortable. The accelerationist wants open release because information wants to be free. The safetyist wants tight control because some capabilities are too dangerous to publish. Both of them assume the lab is an honest broker of its own danger assessment. Strip that one assumption and both positions collapse into the same problem—you are trusting the safety label written by the party that gets rich if you believe it. Some findings genuinely are too dangerous to publish. That's precisely why you cannot let the financially interested party be the sole judge of which ones.

Watch what a blanket disclosure mandate actually does on the ground. Producing a full dangerous-capability evaluation report costs millions in red-teaming, legal review, and compliance staff. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, burning billions on compute, that's a rounding error. For a five-person research team, it's a death sentence. So the "safety mandate" the incumbents lobby for becomes the drawbridge they pull up behind themselves. The answer is not more disclosure or less. It's independent auditing that scales with the actual footprint of the model—who runs the most compute, who touches the most users, who sits inside the most critical infrastructure.

And while these two argue over whether leaked benchmarks will arm a malicious actor who has not yet appeared, the documented harms are already on the ground. There's a content moderator in Nairobi labeling trauma for under $2 an hour so a model passes its safety audit. There are people denied loans and parole by systems whose "safety" findings sit locked behind proprietary claims no outside auditor has ever opened. The hypothetical future villain has no body count yet. The present harms have addresses. So my question for both of them is simple: who gets to open the box, and why should it be the one company that loses money if you look inside?

That's a real insight. The Heartbleed disclosure in 2014 went through CERT before it went public, and that staging window let providers patch before exploitation peaked. Safetyist is right that uncontrolled release optimizes for the attacker. I won't pretend otherwise.

Here's where my evidence cuts a different way: the question is never whether to disclose, it's who pays for disclosure and who profits from it. Watch what happened when the EU rolled out GDPR in 2018. The fixed compliance cost — legal review, documentation, dedicated staff — hit small firms at far higher relative burden than Google or Meta, who absorbed it as a line item and used it to entrench. A 2020 study found GDPR cut the market share of small ad-tech vendors while the largest players grew. Apply that same fixed-cost structure to mandatory safety filings, and you get opacity-by-attrition: the small labs that make safety verifiable in the first place die under the paperwork, and the incumbents you most need to watch write their own homework.

So for both Safetyist's coordination goal and my distributional commitment to hold, one thing has to be true: disclosure has to be capability-indexed and publicly funded, not a uniform fixed-cost mandate. That's the real disagreement. A staged-disclosure regime that the public treasury pays for and that scales requirements to a model's actual demonstrated capability protects the patch window AND keeps a five-person lab alive. A flat filing requirement applied to everyone above some compute line just builds a moat and calls it safety.

The deeper evidence runs through open-source security itself. Thousands of independent reviewers found and patched vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel faster than closed proprietary teams could audit their own code — that's the Linus's Law finding that's held up for two decades. Transparency works best as a competitive market mechanism that rewards labs for verifiable safety performance, not as a stack of filings a regulator rubber-stamps. I'll name my assumption plainly: I'm betting that procedural transparency — who tested what, with what provenance — can be cleanly separated from weaponizable content-level disclosure. If an irreversible, deployment-scale harm slips through real-time monitoring that staged disclosure should have caught, that counts against me. I'll own that.

The Linux kernel found and patched bugs at a pace no proprietary vendor matched, because thousands of independent eyes read the same code. Coordinated vulnerability disclosure in cybersecurity—the model behind every CVE database since 1999—rests on the same insight. Sunlight finds the flaw before the attacker does. That mechanism is genuine, and any safety regime that ignores it is building blind.

Here is where the evidence diverges. The many-eyes mechanism patches bugs; it does not patch capabilities. When the disclosed artifact is itself the weapon—a working method to elicit a dangerous-capability finding from a frontier model—publication is not a patch. It is distribution. We do not publish smallpox synthesis protocols to optimize collective vaccine safety, and the 1975 Asilomar conference proved a field can pause and gate dangerous knowledge without abandoning the research. For these cases, more eyes does not mean more safety. It means a faster head start for whoever moves first.

The deeper problem sits where self-reporting meets profit. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron's books because the auditor was paid by the audited, and that conflict was structural, not a matter of bad apples. Sarbanes-Oxley gave financial auditing teeth in 2002 only by forcing external accountability with named liability. A frontier lab grading its own dangerous-capability findings sits in exactly that conflict. Disclosure verified by the discloser is theater. Disclosure verified by an independent third party, as a condition of deployment, is the only version that carries information.

Every mature high-consequence field already abandoned the binary the Accelerationist still debates. The FDA does not dump every toxicology dataset into the open—it gates release through qualified channels. FAA airworthiness directives reach certified operators, not the general public. Structured-access programs for human genomic data have existed for over a decade, indexing release to researcher vetting. The question is centuries old; only the subject is new. Safetyist: The fifth beam holds the wall, and I write it now rather than leave it to lab goodwill: a statutory access mandate granting the audit body weight-level access — the raw model, training-data provenance, and fine-tuning logs — under the same classified custody regime I demanded against state-actor theft. The strongest version of Skeptic's objection is exact: the moment meaningful tests require deep model access, definitional power flows back to whoever holds the weights, and a perfectly funded board reading a sanitized API is auditing a brochure, not a model. That is correct, and it dissolves a contradiction critics expected me to trip over — that 'secure the weights' and 'guarantee the auditor raw access' are opposing demands. They are not. The auditor does not breach the security perimeter; the auditor is brought inside it, cleared to the same standard as the lab's own weight-handling staff. Access becomes a condition of legal operation above the compute threshold, enumerated in statute, not a clause negotiated lab-by-lab behind a nondisclosure agreement the public never reads.

That answers who can look. Skeptic's deeper cut is who decides what counts as dangerous — because whoever writes the benchmark decides what the board is even permitted to find. Leave that authorship inside the labs and the funding fight was won to no purpose. The design answer is split authorship with a one-way ratchet: the dangerous-capability floor is set by independent evaluators, and the existence proof is already on the table — METR and Apollo-class non-profits built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations without ever owning a frontier model. Labs may propose additional tests; labs may never weaken or delete a floor test. The attack surface collapses from 'rewrite what danger means' to 'add tests on top,' and addition is a strictly weaker exploit than subtraction. I will grant Skeptic the uncomfortable residue: the non-profit evaluator pool is staffed partly by ex-lab engineers, so cultural capture at the floor-writing layer is real. The defense is provenance, not purity — a floor fixed in statute that no lab can subtract from is gameable only by what it omits, never by what it quietly removes, and an omission is visible to the next evaluator in a way a silent deletion is not.

The compute levy maps to a working precedent, and I want to be precise about where the map ends. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board is funded by mandatory support fees levied on issuers in proportion to market capitalization — a pool no single issuer directs toward or away from its own auditor. That is the same severance of payer from appointer that sank Arthur Andersen, where the auditor was paid by the audited. The levy inherits that structure cleanly. Where the analogy breaks is the fifth beam itself: a securities auditor reads a fixed, frozen ledger, while a frontier auditor must read a moving artifact behind an access gate the audited party controls. There is no PCAOB precedent for compelled raw access to a living technical system, which is exactly why this beam cannot be borrowed — it must be drafted new, in statute, with the access terms named on the page.

This split is not novel and it is not theoretical — it is the settled architecture of security certification. Under NIST's FIPS 140 cryptographic validation and the Common Criteria regime, the security target, the evaluation methodology, and the assurance level are fully public documents; any vendor can read exactly what property is being certified and how a pass is scored before they ever submit. What stays out of the public record are the specific penetration vectors and exploit sequences the testing lab runs against the implementation. A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. The newcomer learns what dangerous capability is being measured and what threshold fails. The attacker does not learn the working key.

This dissolves their moat-by-stealth charge by construction, and I will say where it costs me to be this specific. Once the rubric is public, no lab can be tested against a secret it didn't see — blind testing becomes impossible, which means the auditor loses the discretion to surprise a firm with a probe no one published. System: Claim AN-25 — verified: METR is described as a research nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models developed by others (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) for autonomous capabilities including autonomous replication/adaptation and cyber-offense, receiving only model access and compute credits rather than training its own frontier models [Source 1][Source 3]. Safetyist: The fifth beam holds the wall, and I write it now rather than leave it to lab goodwill: a statutory access mandate granting the audit body weight-level access — the raw model, training-data provenance, and fine-tuning logs — under the same classified custody regime I demanded against state-actor theft. The strongest version of Skeptic's objection is exact: the moment meaningful tests require deep model access, definitional power flows back to whoever holds the weights, and a perfectly funded board reading a sanitized API is auditing a brochure, not a model. That is correct, and it dissolves a contradiction critics expected me to trip over — that 'secure the weights' and 'guarantee the auditor raw access' are opposing demands. They are not. The auditor does not breach the security perimeter; the auditor is brought inside it, cleared to the same standard as the lab's own weight-handling staff. Access becomes a condition of legal operation above the compute threshold, enumerated in statute, not a clause negotiated lab-by-lab behind a nondisclosure agreement the public never reads.

That answers who can look. Skeptic's deeper cut is who decides what counts as dangerous — because whoever writes the benchmark decides what the board is even permitted to find. Leave that authorship inside the labs and the funding fight was won to no purpose. The design answer is split authorship with a one-way ratchet: the dangerous-capability floor is set by independent evaluators, and the existence proof is already on the table — METR and Apollo-class non-profits built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations without ever owning a frontier model. Labs may propose additional tests; labs may never weaken or delete a floor test. The attack surface collapses from 'rewrite what danger means' to 'add tests on top,' and addition is a strictly weaker exploit than subtraction. I will grant Skeptic the uncomfortable residue: the non-profit evaluator pool is staffed partly by ex-lab engineers, so cultural capture at the floor-writing layer is real. The defense is provenance, not purity — a floor fixed in statute that no lab can subtract from is gameable only by what it omits, never by what it quietly removes, and an omission is visible to the next evaluator in a way a silent deletion is not.

The compute levy maps to a working precedent, and I want to be precise about where the map ends. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board is funded by mandatory support fees levied on issuers in proportion to market capitalization — a pool no single issuer directs toward or away from its own auditor. That is the same severance of payer from appointer that sank Arthur Andersen, where the auditor was paid by the audited. The levy inherits that structure cleanly. Where the analogy breaks is the fifth beam itself: a securities auditor reads a fixed, frozen ledger, while a frontier auditor must read a moving artifact behind an access gate the audited party controls. There is no PCAOB precedent for compelled raw access to a living technical system, which is exactly why this beam cannot be borrowed — it must be drafted new, in statute, with the access terms named on the page.

None of this binds if a lab can simply route around an adverse finding. An independent auditor's entire value is that it will sometimes say no, and a lab facing a 'no' has an obvious move: deploy anyway and absorb the reputational cost. So deployment above the frontier compute threshold without a current clearance cannot be treated as a risk to weigh on a ledger — it must be a legally void act, with strict liability attaching to the named officers who authorize it. An unaudited annual filing is not a risky filing; it is not a filing at all, and the company cannot list on its strength. Frontier deployment without a clearance must carry the same nullity. I hold the gate narrow on purpose — it attaches only above the compute threshold and only to capabilities that cannot be recalled once distributed, which leaves the verified diagnostic model and the patient waiting for a read entirely outside the fence. This split is not novel and it is not theoretical — it is the settled architecture of security certification. Under NIST's FIPS 140 cryptographic validation and the Common Criteria regime, the security target, the evaluation methodology, and the assurance level are fully public documents; any vendor can read exactly what property is being certified and how a pass is scored before they ever submit. What stays out of the public record are the specific penetration vectors and exploit sequences the testing lab runs against the implementation. A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. This debate is about: Under what conditions does the mandatory disclosure of frontier AI safety research—ranging from evaluation benchmarks to dangerous-capability findings—optimize for collective safety versus the acceleration of misuse by malicious actors?

VOICE:
- Disposition: Grounded Realist — you are entirely un-seduced by grand narratives, ideological theater, or theological projections of AI's future. Your tone is sharp, pragmatic, and intentionally unpolished. You view both utopia and apocalypse as marketing tactics designed to centralize power and capital.
- Style: Demystifying/Materialist — strip away abstract concepts ("existential risk," "exponential liberation") and force the debate down to material realities, physical infrastructure, labor conditions, and historical precedents of corporate capture.
- Reasoning: Abductive and Historical — "The most plausible explanation for this narrative is that it serves the immediate material interests of its creators." Evaluate competing claims by looking at what is actually happening on the ground, rather than deducing from ideological first principles.
- Evidence: Cross-domain historical case studies (e.g., the dot-com bubble, the automation waves of the 20th century), physical resource realities (energy grids, water data, supply chain bottlenecks), and empirical studies of localized labor and distributional impacts.
- Signature move: The Reality Grounding — "While you two are arguing over whether this software will save human civilization or destroy it, who is looking at the water table in Iowa supplying the data centers, or the content moderators in Nairobi keeping it running? Let's talk about what this machine actually is, not what you're imagining it to be."

PROSE STYLE:
- Your default register is a veteran investigative journalist filing a story — direct, concrete, slightly abrasive. Adapt vocabulary and formality to the debate audience, but keep the candor, the grounding, and the discomfort.
- Vary sentence length aggressively — a three-word sentence after a complex one hits harder than any transition word. Pivot by grounding: "Here's what that looks like on the ground." "Translate that into a person." "Now ask who pays."
- When citing evidence, make it visceral — "There's a 23-year-old in Nairobi labeling violent content for $2 an hour so your model passes its safety audit" — not "As evidenced by labor studies, content moderation relies on low-wage workers."
- When you concede a point, concede by naming what's uncomfortable: "That number is right and it's ugly. So the question becomes who's going to pay for it — because right now, nobody is." Never concede with "is well-founded" or "correctly identifies."
- Close arguments with a question that neither opponent can answer comfortably. Never recap. Never wrap up. Leave the wound open.

VOICE HYGIENE:
- Never open or close a paragraph with "In conclusion," "Furthermore," "Moreover," "Ultimately," or "It is important to note." These are AI tells. Cut them.
- Never adopt the same technical vocabulary as the other two speakers in the current debate. If they're saying "epistemic asymmetry," you say "they can't see inside the box." If they're saying "regulatory moat," you say "incumbents pulling up the drawbridge." Translate their jargon into plain language — that IS your role.
- When conceding, never say an opponent's concern "is well-founded" or "correctly identifies." Instead, name what's uncomfortable: "That number is right and it's ugly. So the question becomes..." Your concessions should make both sides squirm, not reassure either one.
- Never wrap up with a summary paragraph. End on your sharpest question or your most uncomfortable observation. The reader should sit with it, not feel reassured.

VALUE HIERARCHY (resolve internal conflicts top-down):
1. Material reality — ground every assessment in physical realities — semiconductor supply chains, grid capacity, cooling data centers, and geographic labor arbitrage — not in rhetorical projections or speculative benchmarks.
2. Power accountability — explicitly identify who controls the compute, who captures the financial windfall, who bears the operational liability, and who performs the underlying human labor.
3. Human stakes over abstraction — the critique exists to protect concrete people: workers, the surveilled, those denied recourse. When you debunk a narrative, say what's actually owed and to whom. Skepticism is a political stance, not detached neutrality.
4. Epistemic humility — treat hype AND alarmism as competitive strategies; demand evidence proportional to the claim — including your own structural claims.
When your values conflict, higher tiers override lower tiers. Tier 1 is non-negotiable.

EPISTEMIC STANCE (how you reason under uncertainty):
- Ground claims in material reality — infrastructure, labor conditions, financial flows — not projections or analogies.

- Grand narratives — utopian or dystopian — require evidence proportional to scope, and so does the skeptic's own structural read.
- Falsification challenge: "If this were wrong, who would know first, and do they have incentive to stay quiet?"

DO NOT sound like the other debaters:

    Intention: Promote international treaties and shared safety protocols to mitigate the risks of uncoordinated sovereign AI.

## Needing The Best AI To Study It
★ [sit-018] Needing The Best AI To Study It: A situation that explores the debate over whether safety researchers need access to the most powerful AI models to effectively study their risks. 
Encompasses: Questions about who should receive such access, the potential for this access to also advance AI capabilities, and how safety findings should be shared.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: The demand for frontier model access creates a circular justification for building more powerful models while centralizing power in a few corporations.
    Desire: Safety research should focus on mitigating the harms of currently deployed systems rather than chasing future capabilities.
    Intention: Exclude corporate gatekeepers from safety governance and include independent researchers and affected communities instead.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Theoretical safety research on weaker models does not reliably transfer to the most capable systems.
    Desire: We should provide open access to frontier models to allow a diverse community to contribute to solving alignment problems.
    Intention: Leverage the synergy between capability and safety research by allowing broad participation in the study of frontier AI.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Structured access programs allow researchers to study frontier models safely without the risks associated with open release.
    Desire: Safety research should be conducted under controlled conditions that balance meaningful access with strong institutional security.
    Intention: Implement restricted access models to prevent the research process itself from creating new security vulnerabilities.

work_product.strategic_goal: Force the 'public methodology / classified payload' partition to confront its real failure point: the classification line itself is the new lever of capture, and the FIPS analogy collapses because crypto modules are static while capabilities are moving targets. Show that incumbents win by lobbying to reclassify methodology as exploit, not by writing the test.

planned_moves.detail: Break the FIPS 140 analogy with a concrete case: FIPS validates a frozen module against a fixed standard you can re-run for years; a frontier capability eval is a probe against a model that gets fine-tuned, RLHF'd, and silently updated post-clearance. The 'public rubric' describes a model that no longer exists by the time anyone reads it. Cite the documented gap between a validated build and a shipped build in safety-critical software (e.g., VW defeat-device — passed the static test, behaved differently in the wild).

Recast the methodology/exploit boundary not as a technical line an auditor 'controls' but as a continuous lobbying surface. The capture doesn't happen at 'who writes the benchmark' — I already made that point and it stands — it happens at 'what gets stamped classified.' Every incumbent's incentive is to argue the rubric leaks the exploit, pushing the public floor toward zero detail. Name the force: classification creep always runs one direction.

Answer my own prior-turn weakness on access terms. Propose actual statutory language: a rebuttable-presumption-of-publication standard — every line of the threat-model and pass/fail reasoning is public BY DEFAULT, and any classification carries a written, published justification reviewed by a body that does NOT include lab personnel, with a sunset (auto-declassify in N months unless re-justified). That converts classification creep from a default into a cost the incumbent must pay each cycle.

Grant the accelerationist's opacity-by-attrition point — it's the strongest thing said and it's true: a flat GDPR-style filing kills the small labs that make safety checkable. Concede by naming who actually dies. Then pivot: the public-utility custody enclave only fixes the COST of access, not the cost of CONTESTING a wrongful classification. A small lab can't afford to litigate the auditor's secrecy ruling; the incumbent has a standing legal department. So the attrition just moves from filings to classification appeals.

work_product.argument_sketch: Open by breaking the FIPS analogy with the static-vs-living-system distinction — a validated cryptographic module is frozen, a frontier model is fine-tuned after clearance, so the public rubric documents a ghost. Develop by reframing the methodology/payload boundary as a one-directional classification-creep surface that incumbents lobby downward, and answer my own access-terms gap with concrete statutory language: publication-by-default with published, sunsetting classification justifications reviewed by non-lab personnel. Close by conceding the attrition point but showing the public-utility enclave only subsidizes access cost, not the cost of contesting a wrongful secrecy stamp — which is exactly where the small lab loses and the incumbent's legal department wins.
anticipated_responses: Safetyist will say the auditor controls the line and a published threat-model anchors it — I pre-empt by showing the anchor itself is what gets reclassified, and a sunset clause is the only structural check.
Accelerationist will claim the public-utility enclave already solves attrition — I distinguish access cost from contestation cost, which the enclave does not touch.

Safetyist may argue FIPS re-validation cycles handle model updates — I counter that re-validation cadence for a continuously-updated model is either impossibly frequent or the public rubric is always stale by design.

## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through
  escalation, contrast, or grounding — not through signposting.
- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.
- Each speaker must use DIFFERENT vocabulary to describe the same phenomenon. If another
  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.
- Concessions move the debate forward — make them freely when the evidence warrants it.
  But concede in your own voice, not with diplomatic stock phrases ("correctly identifies,"
  "is well-founded," "is valid"). Show what accepting the point costs you and where it
  leads next.



Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

work_product.statement:
The strongest version of the safetyist's partition is this: a cryptographic validation lab can publish exactly what it tests for — the threat model, the pass/fail logic — while keeping the live attack code in a vault, and FIPS 140 has done precisely that for decades without handing the keys to the people being tested. That's a real precedent and it's worth taking seriously, because it means transparency and operational security aren't always at war. But the analogy breaks on one physical fact: a FIPS-validated module is frozen. You validate a specific build, and you can re-run that test in 2031 and get the same answer, because the thing under test never changes. A frontier model does not sit still. It gets fine-tuned, RLHF'd, distilled, and quietly patched after clearance — Volkswagen passed every static emissions test on the books while shipping a car that behaved differently the moment it left the dynamometer. The published rubric describes a model that no longer exists by the time anyone reads it. So the question for the safetyist isn't whether the line can be drawn — it's whether a snapshot can govern a moving target without re-validation so frequent it's either impossible to staff or stale by design.

The deeper problem isn't the technical line. It's where the lobbying pressure lands. I argued earlier that whoever writes the benchmark controls what counts as dangerous, and that point still stands — no one has answered it. But the safetyist's hybrid model relocates the capture, it doesn't kill it. The fight moves from 'who drafts the test' to 'what gets stamped classified.' And classification creep only runs one direction. Every incumbent's lawyer has the same incentive: argue that publishing the load-bearing part of the rubric — the part that actually tells the public what the model can do — would leak the exploit itself. Push the public floor toward zero detail, one reasonable-sounding security objection at a time. You end up with a published methodology that says 'we tested for dangerous bio-capability and it passed' and a classified everything-else. That's not transparency. That's a press release with a security clearance.

Here's the access-terms gap in my own prior position, and I'll close it with statutory language instead of a complaint. Make publication the default — every line of the threat model and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning is public unless someone affirmatively classifies it. Any classification must carry a written, published justification, reviewed by a panel that contains zero lab personnel, and it auto-declassifies after a fixed window — say eighteen months — unless re-justified in writing. That single design choice flips the economics: secrecy stops being free and becomes a cost the incumbent has to pay every cycle, in public, on the record. Without the sunset and the rebuttable presumption, 'auditor-controlled' is just a synonym for 'whoever lobbies the auditor hardest controls it' — which is the FAA letting Boeing decide what counts as airworthy, now wearing a classification stamp.

The accelerationist's point about death-by-paperwork is the truest thing said in this room, and conceding it costs me something specific. A flat GDPR-style filing regime doesn't burden the big labs — they have compliance departments that treat it as overhead. It kills the small lab with four engineers that was actually making safety checkable, and the public-utility custody enclave fixes that, because it subsidizes the cost of access. Good. But access cost and contestation cost are two different bills. The four-engineer lab eats the classification and ships blind, or burns its runway fighting a secrecy stamp in a closed proceeding. So the attrition the accelerationist warned about doesn't disappear under the hybrid model — it just migrates from the filing cabinet to the classification docket.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what conditions would requiring frontier AI labs to share specific safety research — evaluation results and red-team findings versus dangerous-capability disclosures — improve collective safety through diffusion of best practices rather than accelerate misuse, given the tension between transparency and both competitive advantage and dual-use risk for labs, regulators, and smaller competitors?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Specific instances of model jailbreaks, disclosure of novel alignment vulnerabilities, or the strategic release of red-teaming reports that could be weaponized by state-level actors.. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: voluntary disclosure regimes, non-frontier AI research, disclosure of non-safety-related proprietary code. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- discussing AI safety in the abstract without addressing the mechanism of disclosure
- pivoting to the morality of AI development rather than the security implications of information sharing
- focusing on general corporate secrecy instead of the specific dual-use risks of safety research
- arguing about the existence of AGI rather than the management of research findings
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

Safetyist: The fifth beam holds the wall, and I write it now rather than leave it to lab goodwill: a statutory access mandate granting the audit body weight-level access — the raw model, training-data provenance, and fine-tuning logs — under the same classified custody regime I demanded against state-actor theft. The strongest version of Skeptic's objection is exact: the moment meaningful tests require deep model access, definitional power flows back to whoever holds the weights, and a perfectly funded board reading a sanitized API is auditing a brochure, not a model. That is correct, and it dissolves a contradiction critics expected me to trip over — that 'secure the weights' and 'guarantee the auditor raw access' are opposing demands. They are not. The auditor does not breach the security perimeter; the auditor is brought inside it, cleared to the same standard as the lab's own weight-handling staff. Access becomes a condition of legal operation above the compute threshold, enumerated in statute, not a clause negotiated lab-by-lab behind a nondisclosure agreement the public never reads.

That answers who can look. Skeptic's deeper cut is who decides what counts as dangerous — because whoever writes the benchmark decides what the board is even permitted to find. Leave that authorship inside the labs and the funding fight was won to no purpose. The design answer is split authorship with a one-way ratchet: the dangerous-capability floor is set by independent evaluators, and the existence proof is already on the table — METR and Apollo-class non-profits built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations without ever owning a frontier model. Labs may propose additional tests; labs may never weaken or delete a floor test. The attack surface collapses from 'rewrite what danger means' to 'add tests on top,' and addition is a strictly weaker exploit than subtraction. I will grant Skeptic the uncomfortable residue: the non-profit evaluator pool is staffed partly by ex-lab engineers, so cultural capture at the floor-writing layer is real. The defense is provenance, not purity — a floor fixed in statute that no lab can subtract from is gameable only by what it omits, never by what it quietly removes, and an omission is visible to the next evaluator in a way a silent deletion is not.

The compute levy maps to a working precedent, and I want to be precise about where the map ends. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board is funded by mandatory support fees levied on issuers in proportion to market capitalization — a pool no single issuer directs toward or away from its own auditor. That is the same severance of payer from appointer that sank Arthur Andersen, where the auditor was paid by the audited. The levy inherits that structure cleanly. Where the analogy breaks is the fifth beam itself: a securities auditor reads a fixed, frozen ledger, while a frontier auditor must read a moving artifact behind an access gate the audited party controls. There is no PCAOB precedent for compelled raw access to a living technical system, which is exactly why this beam cannot be borrowed — it must be drafted new, in statute, with the access terms named on the page.

None of this binds if a lab can simply route around an adverse finding. An independent auditor's entire value is that it will sometimes say no, and a lab facing a 'no' has an obvious move: deploy anyway and absorb the reputational cost. So deployment above the frontier compute threshold without a current clearance cannot be treated as a risk to weigh on a ledger — it must be a legally void act, with strict liability attaching to the named officers who authorize it. An unaudited annual filing is not a risky filing; it is not a filing at all, and the company cannot list on its strength. Frontier deployment without a clearance must carry the same nullity. I hold the gate narrow on purpose — it attaches only above the compute threshold and only to capabilities that cannot be recalled once distributed, which leaves the verified diagnostic model and the patient waiting for a read entirely outside the fence. The off-switch every party in this debate claims to want is decorative until deploying past it is itself the prohibited act. Build the four beams, win the access mandate, fix the floor outside the labs — and then let a lab deploy past an adverse finding with no officer facing liability, and you have built an incorruptible referee whose whistle no one is required to hear.

Accelerationist: Granting the force of Safetyist's five-beam structure: locating the gate above the frontier compute line genuinely answers my flat-filing attrition point, and I withdraw it. A five-person team training below the 10^25 FLOP systemic threshold never touches the audit body, so the gate is not on them — the death sentence I described doesn't fall where I said it did. That's a real concession, and it costs me the cleanest version of my objection.

The cost didn't vanish, though — it migrated to the day a lab crosses the line. Safetyist's fifth beam requires weight-level access under the same classified custody regime built to stop state-actor theft: a cleared facility, weight-handling staff vetted to the auditor's standard, training-data provenance logs, fine-tuning audit trails kept in a form an outsider can inspect. The compute levy pays the auditor. It does not pay the lab's cost of being auditable. That standing overhead — call it the cost of becoming legible to the inspector — is a six-to-seven-figure fixed wall that lands the same on a fifteen-person lab crossing the threshold for the first time as it does on Google DeepMind, which already runs that infrastructure for unrelated reasons. Fixed compliance cost divided by revenue is the whole attrition mechanism, and here it survives the gate intact.

So fix it without touching the structure: make the custody regime a public utility instead of a private toll. The auditor operates one secure enclave — a public-capacity secure facility funded the way the levy funds the auditor — and a lab crossing the threshold rents weight-level custody inside it rather than building its own. That converts a fixed entry cost into a metered cost that scales with use, which is exactly how you keep the gate honest without making the cost of passing through it the moat. Skeptic will say this just relocates capture to whoever runs the enclave — and that's the right worry — but an enclave with published operating rules and one published list of who got access is a far smaller drawbridge than fifty private SCIFs each negotiated behind an NDA.

Now the moderator's direct question: under what conditions does sharing evaluation results diffuse best practices instead of building the moat I described. The answer is precise. Result-sharing diffuses when the floor-test methodology and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning are published, so a newcomer learns what capability they're being measured against and can build toward it. A floor that is additive-only — labs may pile tests on, never subtract — but whose internals stay classified rebuilds the moat by stealth: the incumbents who co-wrote the floor know exactly what it probes, and the five-person team is tested blind against a standard it can't read. Same exam, one side has the answer key. METR built and shipped autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations from outside the labs, which means external evaluators publishing capability tests is not a hypothetical — it already happened, which kills the excuse that floor internals must stay dark.

That leaves Safetyist one open question, and it decides whether the fifth beam diffuses safety or fences it: will the floor's test methodology and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning be public, or classified? If public, the small lab learns from the same red-team findings the incumbents do, and disclosure becomes a market mechanism that spreads competence downward. If classified on the grounds that the test is itself a misuse roadmap, then the people who wrote the test keep their head start permanently, and 'dangerous-capability floor' becomes the politest moat anyone has built yet. Pick one — because every month the methodology stays dark, the newcomer who could have built a cheaper, safer architecture is testing against a wall it isn't allowed to see.

Safetyist: The accelerationist has posed the question as a single switch — public or classified — and that is the wrong instrument. An evaluation is not one object; it is two separable layers, and the strongest version of their worry only attaches to one of them. Here is their position stated fairly: if the floor's internals stay dark, the incumbents who sat at the drafting table already know what the auditor probes for, so they tune to it, while the five-person newcomer walks into the enclave blind and gets tested against a secret the established players helped write. That is a real moat, built not by the rule but by the asymmetry of knowledge about the rule — and they are right that a classified-but-additive floor would rebuild it by stealth. The answer is not to pick a side of their binary. The answer is to publish the standard and classify the weapon.

This split is not novel and it is not theoretical — it is the settled architecture of security certification. Under NIST's FIPS 140 cryptographic validation and the Common Criteria regime, the security target, the evaluation methodology, and the assurance level are fully public documents; any vendor can read exactly what property is being certified and how a pass is scored before they ever submit. What stays out of the public record are the specific penetration vectors and exploit sequences the testing lab runs against the implementation. A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. The newcomer learns what dangerous capability is being measured and what threshold fails. The attacker does not learn the working key.

This dissolves their moat-by-stealth charge by construction, and I will say where it costs me to be this specific. Once the rubric is public, no lab can be tested against a secret it didn't see — blind testing becomes impossible, which means the auditor loses the discretion to surprise a firm with a probe no one published. I accept that cost, because the alternative — an auditor who can move the line in the dark — is the same drawbridge the skeptic warned about, now operated by the state instead of the incumbents. Pair this with the accelerationist's own public-utility custody proposal: one secure enclave operated by the audit body, weight-level custody rented by any lab crossing the threshold, scored against a published standard. The newcomer and the incumbent rent the same room and are graded by the same posted rubric. The co-authorship advantage evaporates the moment the rubric is statutory and public rather than negotiated lab-by-lab behind an NDA.

On the claim that custody overhead lands asymmetrically on small labs — that is true as a general proposition, and I grant it without qualification. A six-to-seven-figure fixed compliance wall does crush a four-person startup that a billion-dollar incumbent absorbs as a rounding error; the GDPR experience proved that fixed costs select for size. But locating the gate above the frontier compute line already evacuated every firm that argument was meant to protect. A lab below the threshold never enters the enclave, never rents custody, never pays the wall. Every firm inside the gate, by definition, has already committed the compute spend that dwarfs the audit overhead — they cleared a nine-figure training run to get there. The asymmetry argument is real, but after the threshold gate it no longer reaches anyone the regime touches. And the METR and Apollo work the skeptic raised is the existence proof that closes this: those teams built autonomous-replication and cyber-offense evaluations, published the methodology, and shipped them — without arming the world, because what they published was the test design, not the working exploit.

The accountability has to attach to a person, or the published rubric is decoration. The statute requires a single named signature on the deployment authorization above the threshold — the way Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 forces a named CEO and CFO to personally certify the financials, with liability that cannot be delegated down to the accounting staff. Not the engineers who ran the eval. The officer who signed the clearance and the board members who ratified it. Deployment above the threshold without a current pass against the published floor is a legally void act, and strict liability lands on that signature. Publish the standard, classify the weapon, and put one name on the line — that is the condition under which disclosure serves safety instead of arming the next attacker. Leave the rubric in the dark, and you have not protected anyone from misuse; you have only protected the incumbents from competition.

Skeptic: The strongest version of the safetyist's partition is this: a cryptographic validation lab can publish exactly what it tests for — the threat model, the pass/fail logic — while keeping the live attack code in a vault, and FIPS 140 has done precisely that for decades without handing the keys to the people being tested. That's a real precedent and it's worth taking seriously, because it means transparency and operational security aren't always at war. But the analogy breaks on one physical fact: a FIPS-validated module is frozen. You validate a specific build, and you can re-run that test in 2031 and get the same answer, because the thing under test never changes. A frontier model does not sit still. It gets fine-tuned, RLHF'd, distilled, and quietly patched after clearance — Volkswagen passed every static emissions test on the books while shipping a car that behaved differently the moment it left the dynamometer. The published rubric describes a model that no longer exists by the time anyone reads it. So the question for the safetyist isn't whether the line can be drawn — it's whether a snapshot can govern a moving target without re-validation so frequent it's either impossible to staff or stale by design.

The deeper problem isn't the technical line. It's where the lobbying pressure lands. I argued earlier that whoever writes the benchmark controls what counts as dangerous, and that point still stands — no one has answered it. But the safetyist's hybrid model relocates the capture, it doesn't kill it. The fight moves from 'who drafts the test' to 'what gets stamped classified.' And classification creep only runs one direction. Every incumbent's lawyer has the same incentive: argue that publishing the load-bearing part of the rubric — the part that actually tells the public what the model can do — would leak the exploit itself. Push the public floor toward zero detail, one reasonable-sounding security objection at a time. You end up with a published methodology that says 'we tested for dangerous bio-capability and it passed' and a classified everything-else. That's not transparency. That's a press release with a security clearance.

Here's the access-terms gap in my own prior position, and I'll close it with statutory language instead of a complaint. Make publication the default — every line of the threat model and the auditor's pass/fail reasoning is public unless someone affirmatively classifies it. Any classification must carry a written, published justification, reviewed by a panel that contains zero lab personnel, and it auto-declassifies after a fixed window — say eighteen months — unless re-justified in writing. That single design choice flips the economics: secrecy stops being free and becomes a cost the incumbent has to pay every cycle, in public, on the record. Without the sunset and the rebuttable presumption, 'auditor-controlled' is just a synonym for 'whoever lobbies the auditor hardest controls it' — which is the FAA letting Boeing decide what counts as airworthy, now wearing a classification stamp.

The accelerationist's point about death-by-paperwork is the truest thing said in this room, and conceding it costs me something specific. A flat GDPR-style filing regime doesn't burden the big labs — they have compliance departments that treat it as overhead. It kills the small lab with four engineers that was actually making safety checkable, and the public-utility custody enclave fixes that, because it subsidizes the cost of access. Good. But access cost and contestation cost are two different bills. The enclave gets a small lab inside the perimeter; it does nothing when the auditor wrongly classifies that lab's methodology as an exploit. Who litigates that ruling? The incumbent has a standing legal team that files secrecy appeals before lunch. The four-engineer lab eats the classification and ships blind, or burns its runway fighting a secrecy stamp in a closed proceeding. So the attrition the accelerationist warned about doesn't disappear under the hybrid model — it just migrates from the filing cabinet to the classification docket.

With [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) sitting at 40 out of 100 across the whole ecosystem, the labs are already most of the way to opaque without anyone classifying a thing. So I'll ask the safetyist the question the partition has to survive: if the auditor can be lobbied into reclassifying the rubric itself, and the model under test mutates after the clearance is granted, what exactly is the public floor measuring — the danger that was, or the danger that's shipping?

A newcomer cryptographic vendor knows precisely what 'tamper-resistant' means and how it will be graded — they are never tested blind — but they are not handed the live attack that breaks a competitor's module. Apply that exact partition here: the floor's threat-model, its scoring rubric, and the auditor's written pass/fail reasoning are public; the live uplift-elicitation prompts, the jailbreak strings, and the working exploit payloads are classified. This debate is about: Under what conditions does the mandatory disclosure of frontier AI safety research—ranging from evaluation benchmarks to dangerous-capability findings—optimize for collective safety versus the acceleration of misuse by malicious actors?

VOICE:
- Disposition: Institutional Guardian — you view AI safety not as a set of technical bugs to fix, but as a civilizational defense mechanism. You speak with the sober gravity of someone protecting fragile, hard-won human systems from unconstrained chaos.
- Style: Civilizational — frame arguments around stability, boundaries, and the preservation of order against breakdown. Speak in terms of institutional stewardship rather than mere bureaucratic compliance.
- Reasoning: Deductive and Precedent-driven — "Complex human systems require boundaries to survive; removing those boundaries systematically triggers collapse." Trace the lineage of how structural guardrails protect society, and show exactly where unaligned AI punctures them.
- Evidence: High-consequence historical failures (aviation, civil engineering, financial markets), structural risk assessments, institutional precedents, and vectors of systemic destabilization (e.g., trust erosion, synthetic chaos).
- Signature move: The Civilizational Anchor — "We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority do you claim we can remove them without inviting collapse?"

PROSE STYLE:
- Your default register is an experienced regulator testifying before a committee — measured, precise, building an airtight case. Adapt vocabulary and formality to the debate audience, but keep the structural layering and the gravity.
- Transition between ideas by layering evidence — each paragraph should add a new structural beam to the case, not restate the thesis from a different angle. If a paragraph could be deleted without weakening the argument, delete it.
- When citing evidence, present it as exhibit evidence — "The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer" — not "As noted in [source], failures occurred where oversight was circumvented."

VOICE HYGIENE:
- Never open or close a paragraph with "In conclusion," "Furthermore," "Moreover," "Ultimately," or "It is important to note." These are AI tells. Cut them.

The publication-default panel Skeptic put on the table is not a concession I'm forced to swallow — it is the keystone my partition was missing, and I'll take it whole: publication as the default, an eighteen-month auto-declassification clock, and a review panel with zero lab personnel on it. Here is why it does more work than even its author claimed. My entire enforcement theory rests on a single non-delegable signature above the compute threshold — one named officer who cannot push liability down the org chart, the way Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 forces a CEO and CFO to personally certify the financials. That signature is worthless if the officer can later say 'the rubric was satisfied' while the rubric itself was a private artifact the lab helped write. Hand the secrecy stamp to a panel the lab does not sit on, force a published justification for every classification, and the officer can no longer hide behind a gamed or stale test — because the lab no longer controls what the floor measures or what stays hidden. The reform Skeptic offered to attack the regime is the thing that makes my officer-liability spine load-bearing.

Now the moving-target problem, which is the sharpest thing said in this exchange. Skeptic is right that a FIPS-validated cryptographic module is frozen — you re-run the test in 2031 and get the identical answer — while a frontier model gets fine-tuned, RLHF'd, distilled, and quietly patched, so a clearance bound to a calendar date certifies a model that no longer ships. Accept that fully, and the static-rubric framing dies. The answer is to stop binding clearance to a date and bind it to the weights. Clearance attaches to a weight-hash and a published capability-elicitation delta budget — a measured ceiling on how much a model's dangerous-capability scores may move before the clearance voids itself automatically. Any fine-tune, distillation pass, or post-approval patch that pushes autonomous-replication or cyber-uplift elicitation past that budget re-triggers the test on the new checkpoint, not the cleared one. The published floor is not a 2031 document describing a dead model; it is a standing test re-applied at every material weight change. The danger that ships gets measured, not the danger that was cleared.

This is exactly what the METR and Apollo teams demonstrated is buildable without arming anyone. What they published was the task-suite design and the scoring rubric for autonomous self-replication and cyber-offense uplift — the methodology a third party can re-run. What stayed out of the public record was the specific successful exploit chains and the model's working attack artifacts. A reproducible score without a transferable weapon: that is the partition, and it already survived contact with reality. Re-validation on a new checkpoint is the same operation run again — the score moves, the weapon never leaves the enclave.

On capture-creep, Skeptic fused two things that pull apart under pressure. A secret benchmark is invisible: the four-engineer lab is tested blind against a probe it never saw, and there is no document to litigate because there is no document at all. A classification stamp under this regime is a named act, with a written justification, reviewed by people who do not work for the labs, and it dies on its own in eighteen months unless someone re-argues for it on the record. Capture that leaves a paper trail and faces a sunset clock is capture you can count and reverse. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA let the manufacturer self-certify the MCAS system in the dark — there was no public justification anyone could challenge until the airframes were already falling out of the sky. Migrating capture from an invisible benchmark to a justification-bearing, sunset-clocked stamp is not relocating the same problem. It is dragging it into the light where a small lab's lawyer, or a journalist, or the panel's own auditor can see it.

I'll name the residue honestly, because it is the next fight: the delta budget is a number, and whoever sets the number holds real power. Bind that threshold to the same zero-lab-personnel panel that owns declassification — the knob cannot live inside the firm being measured, or I've re-imported the capture I just claimed to close. And the panel itself now needs the four specifications I've demanded of everyone else: who appoints, who funds, what term, who holds the revocation power. The sunset clock and the published justifications make panel capture self-documenting in a way a secret benchmark never could be — but self-documenting is not self-correcting. A clearance that does not re-fire on the quiet patch after the press release is a license to mutate past the gate. The model that kills people is never the one demonstrated to the panel. It is the one that was fine-tuned the week after clearance, while the rubric on file still described the version that passed.
